maintopic: PROPOSED AMCHITKA NUCLEAR TEST-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
PROPOSED AMCHITKA NUCLEAR TEST-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to take advantage of Standing Order 43 to move a motion. It is similar to the motion proposed yesterday by my colleague, the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Anderson), and its urgency arises from the fact that within the next few days the President of the United States is to make a final decision on the proposed underground test at Amchitka Island.
The Canadian government and, more specifically, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp), have already expressed Canada's reservations about this proposed test. At this time I think it is important that this House, opposition as well as government members, indicate to President Nixon that we are unanimous and united in our concern about this and any such future tests by any nation.
I would propose that this House formally record its grave concern at continued nuclear weapons testing, wherever such testing may take place; that it regrets the recent high yield underground test in the Soviet Union; that it expresses its hope that the United States government will reconsider its plans to carry out a test on Amchitka Island; and that it strongly reaffirms its support of the efforts being made in the United Nations by Canada and other countries to get international agreement to ban all underground nuclear weapons tests.

subsubtopic: REPRESENTATIONS TO UNITED STATES FOR REMOVAL OF U.S. IMPORT SURTAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister. In view of the statement made by the United States Secretary of the Treasury, Mr. John Connally, in his speech to the International Monetary Fund this morning to the effect that the United States will be prepared to remove its 10

per cent additional levy on dutiable imports if other governments make tangible progress in coming weeks in dismantling their trade barriers and permitting the establishment of realistic currency exchange rates, has the Canadian government indicated to the United States government any willingness to make moves or negotiate in this regard?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: REPRESENTATIONS TO UNITED STATES FOR REMOVAL OF U.S. IMPORT SURTAX
speechtext: Not since the statement was made, Mr. Speaker; it has just come to our attention now. But the House knows that in the past few weeks, and even before, our ministers and officials have been telling the United States that the 10 per cent surcharge should not apply to us, and that we had already done the things mentioned in Mr. Connally's statement to which the hon. member has just referred.

subsubtopic: REPRESENTATIONS TO UNITED STATES FOR REMOVAL OF U.S. IMPORT SURTAX
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, since Mr. Connally has indicated that the United States government is willing to negotiate regarding this matter on a bilateral basis with any country which so desires, is it the intention of the government in the near future to sit down in a session of hard bargaining with the United States government with a view to having the 10 per cent surcharge removed as soon as possible, and will the Prime Minister be willing to participate in these negotiations in order that Canada's position may have the best chance of being understood?

subsubtopic: REPRESENTATIONS TO UNITED STATES FOR REMOVAL OF U.S. IMPORT SURTAX
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for the confidence he has expressed in my negotiating powers.

subsubtopic: REPRESENTATIONS TO UNITED STATES FOR REMOVAL OF U.S. IMPORT SURTAX
speechtext: It is a lack of confidence in your ministers.

subsubtopic: REPRESENTATIONS TO UNITED STATES FOR REMOVAL OF U.S. IMPORT SURTAX
speechtext: All I can do is repeat that this type of discussion has been going on for some weeks. I am not sure whether Secretary Connally wants to embark on a different type of bilateral negotiation, but certainly we have been making representations on our behalf to the United States for some time.

subsubtopic: REPRESENTATIONS TO UNITED STATES FOR REMOVAL OF U.S. IMPORT SURTAX
speechtext: I have a final supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Obviously it would be a good idea to get in touch with Mr. Connally to find out what he does mean. Is it not a fact that one of the principal reasons Canada has not been able to obtain an exemption from the 10 per cent surcharge is the very poor relations between Canada and the United States which this government has engendered during the past year?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: REPRESENTATIONS TO UNITED STATES FOR REMOVAL OF U.S. IMPORT SURTAX
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member's supplementary question is in the form of an argument.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT PROGRAMS TO STIMULATE THE ECONOMY - SUGGESTED NEW MEASURES
speechtext:
This House cannot tolerate any longer the economic policies of the government which have produced massive unemployment that threatens to become more serious this fall and winter; nor can this House tolerate any longer the government's failure to implement policies to reduce Canada's dependence on a single market and to assure a strong and independent Canadian economy.
Therefore this House calls for:
(1)	a large scale program, in co-operation with the provinces and municipalities, to provide jobs this winter for the growing army of unemployed;
(2)	immediate reduction in taxes, particularly for lower and middle income groups;
(3)	further government action to force down interest rates;
(4)	large additional funds for housing;
(5)	essential anti-pollution measures such as funds to municipalities to build waste-treatment plants and other necessary works; and
(6)	introduction of a program designed to protect Canada's future by redirecting trade so that it will not continue to be at the mercy of a single market and by restructuring the economy to free it from foreign domination and control.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I suggest to the House and to the people of Canada that the present economic events in this country have highlighted two urgent facts facing the Canadian people. One is the unfortunate likelihood that unemployment this winter will be at least as severe as last year and probably a great deal more serious. We face the possibility of three quarters of a million or more Canadians out of work in the winter months unless steps to meet the situation are taken by the government without delay. The second fact, which the Nixon economic policies have underlined, is the danger facing our country's future if our economy continues under foreign control and our welfare continues to depend on the benevolence of Washington and of the multinational corporations. For years the NDP has warned of these dangers. At last their existence has been acknowledged by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) and by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson). But there is still no suggestion of policies to free our economy from the straightjacket of foreign domination. I want to deal with each of those facts, as I call them, in turn.
I want to say to the Prime Minister, who is here at the moment, and to the government that as I study the situation I see that instead of presenting to Parliament a program to deal with the present unemployment crisis we
Alleged Failure to Stimulate Economy
have had from the Minister of Finance pollyanna forecasts of which every one has proven wrong. I suggest on a study of the record that either the Minister of Finance should fire his forecasters or he should fire himself for being an easy prey to the defensive, bureaucratic optimism. On second thought, I think perhaps both should happen, the Minister of Finance should fire his advisers and someone should fire him for misleading the Parliament and the country.
When we face this emergency it is important to recall only a few of the minister's alleged predictions. On January 30, 1969, the Minister of Finance said "the latest monthly figures have fallen below 5 per cent", and having said that went on to paint a rosy picture for the rest of that year. What were the facts? The facts were that in October of 1969 the unemployment rate went beyond 5 per cent, that in May, 1970, it went over 6 per cent, and that from May until today it has stayed at over 6 per cent continually for 16 months.
Let me give a second instance. On November 12, 1970,- and hon. members and the people of Canada should listen to this with attention-the Minister of Finance said that unemployment had reached its peak. Everyone in this House knows that since that fatuous statement the unemployment situation has continued bad and has grown worse. On September 7 of this year the Minister of Finance said: "Unemployment will continue to decline". Unfortunately for Canada, one week later the Minister of Finance was shown to be wrong again.
I cite these examples-and I want to come to some statements made by the Prime Minister himself in a moment-because they underline the complacency and the insensitivity of this government toward the major problem that has faced the Canadian people for a year and a half at least. These are merely a few of the minister's pearls. It occurred to me as I was writing my notes that our Minister of Finance has not merely created a credibility gap, he has created a credibility desert. He can never be believed again on any of his statements about the future position of Canada's economy.
The Prime Minister himself and the government, particularly after the disastrous unemployment figures were revealed for the month of August of this year, went on a search to manufacture statistical excuses for the serious unemployment which we have seen in August, and that too in my submission is most reprehensible. I said the other day, in commenting on an answer which the Prime Minister gave me to a question, that he was playing games with the unemployment situation. It was true then, and the points I want to raise now underline the validity and the relevance of my statement.
The Prime Minister discovered, apparently for the first time, in answers to questions in the House in recent days and on a television program the other day that the young, the people aged 14 to 19, were particularly affected by unemployment in this country. Indeed, he said on a number of occasions that this was an unexpected development. I say to the Prime Minister I find that to be an astonishing statement. Indeed, as a member of this House and as a citizen of Canada, I find it embarrassing that the head of our government should make a statement so patently, factually wrong. If he found that to be an unexe-pected phenomenon, I do not know where he has been

September 30, 1971
Alleged Failure to Stimulate Economy
living in the last few months. The facts are that in August, 1971, the number of unemployed between the ages of 14 and 19 was 132,000, and the percentage of unemployed it represented was 29 per cent. But in July, a month earlier, the number was 184,000 and the percentage was 35.8 per cent. In June of this year, two months earlier, the number was 197,000 and the percentage was also 35.8 per cent. In fact, the number and the percentage of unemployment in August among the group between 14 and 19 was lower in August than it had been in June and July.
If the Prime Minister's advisers had taken the trouble to brief him on this, he would have found that the percentage of unemployed among the 14 to 19 group has always been high in the month of August. In the years 1968, 1969 and 1970 they were a little lower than in 1971, and in the years 1965, 1966 and 1967 they were a little higher than in August, 1971. But always the number and the percentage of the unemployed in the 14 to 19 years group in the month of August have been a very large proportion. It is astonishing to me that he should find it an unexpected phenomenon that became evident only in August of this year.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT PROGRAMS TO STIMULATE THE ECONOMY - SUGGESTED NEW MEASURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I heard the Prime Minister deal both with the proportion of unemployed in that age group and the participation rate, and I say to the Prime Minister that if he looks at the participation figures closely he will find that although the participation rate of this age group in August, 1971, was somewhat-not substantially-higher than in August, 1970, it really is not of very great significance when you consider that the participation of the total labour force was a little bit lower this year than last year. I suggest to the Prime Minister that it is not a new phenomenon, not a new development that was suddenly to be discovered, nor by any means was it the most important part of the development.
I am interested merely in underlining the fact that the government, instead of recognizing the severity of the unemployment crisis and saying, "It is bad; let us do something about it," is constantly looking for excuses, as indicated by either the pollyanna statements of the Minister of Finance or the astonishing and embarrassing statements of the Prime Minister.
If I widen this youth group, and I deal with unemployment among the ages 14 to 24, the following facts-I do not often cite statistics but it is important in this case to put them on the record-emerge. In August, 1971, the number unemployed between ages 14 to 24 was 240,000. Their proportion of the total unemployment was 52.7 per cent. In July, the number was 293,000 and the proportion

was 57 per cent. In June, the number was 313,000 and the proportion was 56.7 per cent.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, as I was preparing my notes I remembered, without going back to Hansard, that each time I have referred to unemployment in this country- and I am sure I am right in saying that each time other members of my party as well as members of the Conservative party who have referred to this unemployment-I always pointed out that the largest group suffering as a result of the government's economic policies and as a result of the massive unemployment was the age group between 14 and 19, and the age group between 19 and 24. If I went back through Hansard I could find references to this group in my statements, and in my questions to ministers of the Crown at least a dozen times in the last 12 or 16 months. It is not an unexpected phenomenon. It is an obvious thing that has been happening for the last two years. On various occasions we emphasized that when you throw young people out of school and university into society without any future, any hope, you are creating great dangers for society. I have emphasized that this may be of particular relevance to the situation in the province of Quebec. I say it is not true that this is a new phenomenon, and let not the government try to peddle it as new and unexpected. To do that is either ignorance or dishonesty and, Mr. Speaker, I leave it to you and other Members of Parliament to take your pick.
The government has indulged in other excuses for the present situation. The Prime Minister referred to one of them. Members of the government have talked about an immense increase in the labour force this year. They have talked about increases in the participation rate. On the CBC program to which I referred the Prime Minister said, "There has been more job creation than there ever has been in our economy." Mr. Speaker, without going into the statistics in detail I say that those statements are wrong. They are statistically and historically false, and they are merely a shabby excuse for the government not having taken steps earlier.
If you study them, the statistics show that even when the employment picture was much better than it has been in the last few months, for example, from August, 1964, to August, 1967, when unemployment was somewhere around 3 per cent to 41 per cent, instead of being over 6 per cent as it is now, the growth in the labour force was much higher, and the participation rate was necessarily higher, otherwise we would have had more unemployment. And the number of new jobs created in each of those years was very considerably higher than the number of new jobs created during this present economic crisis.
The reason that I have referred to these statistics is that I want if I can, through you, Sir, through Members of Parliament, through the press-if they are interested-to nail down once and for all these excuses of the Prime Minister, of the Minister of Finance, and of the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Lang) as being false. They are statistically wrong. They are deliberate excuses to hide the inaction and lack of program on the part of the government. Let no one in Canada be fooled by any of these games played by an insensitive government during a highly dangerous and critical unemployment situation. It is obvious to everyone in Canada, except apparently the
September 30, 1971

government, that we face an emergency this winter, and the way to deal with the emergency is to have an emergency program to create jobs this winter. That is why the very first point of the motion I had the honour to move requests that the government immediately undertake a massive program to create jobs this winter.
That cannot be done by the federal government alone. In order to accomplish it, the plans of provincial governments are needed, and the plans of municipal governments. It is not possible for the federal government alone to create a sufficient number of jobs. That can be accomplished only if the provinces and the municipalities are given an opportunity, and are given the funds, the finances, to add to the works that are needed to create the jobs. And they need time, Mr. Speaker. This is why I have been so critical of the Prime Minister about the federal-provincial conferences. And I was delighted to hear this afternoon that at last he found it necessary, or he agreed, or whatever the term may be-if I understood his answers correctly-that he found it desirable to write the provincial governments and ask if they can now attend a conference at an earlier date than December 6 which had previously been agreed to by them.
I appreciate, Mr. Speaker, that the Prime Minister may have to leave the chamber. I am sure he has important work to do, but in the Prime Minister's presence I want to say that my impression of what he has been saying throughout the last number of days on this issue of the federal-provincial conference, from reading the letters that have been made public, is that at no time had the Prime Minister called the provinces to a special conference to deal with unemployment this winter. The Prime Minister called for a conference on non-constitutional matters, on general economic matters. Maybe one is necessary, but at no time did he say to the provinces, "We face an unemployment emergency this winter. We must have a conference on this point. I invite you to such a conference."
The Prime Minister has now left the chamber, Mr. Speaker, and I have to say in his absence that had he had the understanding and the sense of urgency that as the leader of the Canadian government he ought to have had, he should have issued such an invitation for an emergency conference to deal specifically and only with unemployment. I am confident that no government in this country, not even the government of Ontario which is in the midst of an election campaign, would have failed to come to such a conference if such a conference had been called by the Prime Minister of Canada. It is only because the negotiations were for a conference on general economic matters that the normal negotiations about a date and the normal considerations about convenience were taken into account. I am confident, and I repeat, that if the provinces and the municipalities had been called to a conference to deal specifically with the threat of severe unemployment this winter, as they should have been, that conference would now be taking place and not be delayed another day.
The reason for urgency in this regard is obvious to every thinking person. Indeed, you do not need full wit to understand this. Some of those who have less than full wit
Alleged Failure to Stimulate Economy
on the other side could easily understand it as well. They must understand that no province or municipality could participate in a job-creating program for this winter unless the plans are made now. You cannot create jobs for November, December, January, February and March if the programs and plans are announced in October, November or December. You could create jobs for April, May, June and July of next year, but not for this winter at such a late conference. With the knowledge of the facts known to every member of this House and every member of the country, I charge this government once again with complete-perhaps that is an exaggeration-with disastrous unconcern about the unemployment crisis this winter, and I charge it with failure to take at least the initial steps to deal with it by bringing the provinces and the municipalities together to create the necessary programs.
There have been hints by the Prime Minister and other members of the government, and I have seen stories in the newspapers, which suggest that the government is considering producing a program designed, as the Prime Minister has said, to deal with unemployment this winter. If that is done without consultation with the provinces and municipalities it will likely be inadequate. If such an announcement is made, and if the program is at all adequate, I will be pleased and happy to welcome it on behalf of my party. Indeed, I hope the announcement will be made during this debate or, if not during this debate, that it will be announced within the next day or two. Every day's delay in the announcement of that program will make it more difficult for the provinces and the municipalities, as well as public and private corporations, to respond and meet the unemployment crisis this winter.
My motion sets out some other elements which are needed in such a program. I will not bother repeating them in my speech. They are not original suggestions, they have been made on many occasions, not only by me and colleagues in my party, but by other members and economists across the country. They include such things as reducing the income tax for the lower and middle income groups, lowering the interest rate, a massive injection of funds to build the homes which are needed across the country and a massive injection of funds to municipalities to fight pollution in their environment and to build waste treatment plants and other such things. All these things, such as forcing down the interest rates in this country, are known and must be done immediately. They are not original and I do not claim originality for them. They are urgently required and must be urgently applied.
The second point my motion makes and that I ask members of Parliament to take into consideration is that our present crisis is related directly to our dependence on a single market and to the foreign control of our economy. It is not only the unemployment crisis that is involved. That crisis was created by the government itself as a result of its phony war against inflation or its cruel policy of creating unemployment. Our government did that itself and it needed little help. It is now getting a little help from the Nixon economic policy. Undoubtedly, our unemployment situation is threatened further by the effect of the 10 per cent surcharge on the export of manufactured goods and some agricultural goods in this country.

September 30, 1971
Alleged Failure to Stimulate Economy
This additional trouble we have and the general fear which faces Canada are directly tied to the fact that we are in a straitjacket of foreign domination over our economy. I am not saying that were we not in that situation we would not suffer some consequences as a result of the Washington policy. Obviously we would, and obviously every country in the western world has suffered from it, but we would not have the same situation we have in Canada, which is more serious and more frightening than in any other western country, if it were not for our ties to and controls by the United States economy. I appeal to the government and, if I may do so without being presumptuous, to the people of Canada, to awaken to the dangers and act now to start a new orientation for the Canadian economy so we may be free of foreign domination and free from reliance on a single market for our trade. I know this is a long term thing. This cannot be done in the course of a year or, indeed, in the course of five years. This will require a commitment over a period of years, but it must be started now.
The present emergency in Canada has underlined the importance of the problem, and this is the time to begin. This is why it is incomprehensible and heartbreaking to me that we are still waiting for a government statement on its policy on foreign ownership and a statement as to what will be done vis-a-vis the present situation and the threat of the United States economic policy extending beyond the 10 per cent surcharge to DISC and other protectionist policies. It is obvious that Liberal continen-talism dies hard if it dies at all. If this government continues in its continentalist mendicant poise toward the United States this country's political independence, as well as its economic independence, is in a very serious and precarious state.
The Prime Minister said the other day that if the United States wants Canada to be merely a source for its natural resources something will have to be done about the situation. Again I am astonished by the Prime Minister's apparent lack of understanding. I can hardly believe it because he is a highly intelligent and well-trained man and should understand Canada's economic position over the years. He says "if" the United States wants to use us as a resource source; it has used Canada as that and nothing else for decades. We have always played this role for the United States. We have always been the country upon which the United States has relied for its natural resources. It has yanked out our non-renewable resources and shipped them to the United States, in most cases without refining, smelting or dealing with them in any other way in Canada.
Foreign control and reliance upon the United States market for our trade has been a fact of Canadian economic life for literally decades in our history, and that the Prime Minister should still say "if" that is the case is an embarrassment which I as a member of this Parliament have to regret. We must start moving in a new direction. We must say to the people of Canada we are ready for new directions in our economy, and that as legislators and as a government we are ready to proceed in that new direction to set a national purpose in respect of our selfreliance in the Canadian economy, independence from foreign control and domination, and that we start that process today not next year or ten years from now. I am

confident that the Canadian people are ready to take that step. If that step involves some temporary dislocation, as it undoubtedly would, and some temporary costs, as it undoubtedly would, we have the ingenuity and capacity to reduce the dislocation and cost to a minimum and to do the things that are necessary for Canada's future independence.
In my last two minutes-I am informed that is all I have left-I wish to make two points. First, there are obvious steps that must be taken if we are to gain control of the Canadian economy. We must de-emphasize the export of non-renewable resources by removing the tax exemptions and holidays we are now giving to mining and petroleum corporations and by putting a surcharge on the export of oil and gas and similar, non-renewable resources that are in strong demand. We must step up the sale of agricultural and forest products. We must build labour intensive industries. We must rationalize our secondary manufacturing in this country. Above all, we must seek new trading partners, particularly in the developing nations of the world, by buying their commodities and extending to them long term credits. We must stop foreign take overs in this country. We must control foreign equity investment in this country and set up an agency to monitor foreign corporations and make sure that their actions are in the interests of this country.
My last point is this. The time has come for the people of Canada and the members of this parliament to renew their faith in our country. As one travels across this great country one never fails to be impressed. I never fail to be impressed by the immense wealth with which we have been endowed and by Canada's great beauty. I have never visited any other part of the world without feeling that there is equal beauty in this country. There is great wealth and great beauty, as I say. One never fails to be impressed by the great people that are in this country from coast to coast. A country as wealthy and as beautiful as this one, and with people as great as ours, can stand on its own feet. The time has come for us to do just that.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to have the opportunity of being associated with the motion in the name of the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) which incorporates many suggestions that have come from official opposition members and the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) during the last several months.
While reading a few notes in the course of the preliminary preparation for my part in today's debate, I came across a passage printed in Canadian Forum, back in May, 1964. It impressed me so much that I should like to put in on the record. The passage reads as follows:
Our politicians occasionally talk about unemployment, but neither the Federal nor the Provincial authorities have ever categorically declared that they would assume the responsibility of fixing the problem. In fact, the country awaits from all levels of government the elaboration of a new and adequate policy. Among other things, it is inconceivable that politicians should continue to dread budgetary deficits and that, even when resorting to them, they should continue to pay homage to the sacred cow of a balanced budget.
It continues at length in the same vein and then concludes as follows:
September 30, 1971

In effect, such policies would require either a readjustment of the external value of the dollar or a strong injection of foreign capital. Because devaluation and large scale investment from abroad are found to be unacceptable from the nationalistic point of view, the government rejects truly expansionist measures and relies upon ineffectual expedients.
That quotation comes from something that was written by the Committee for Political Realism, and the author was Pierre Elliott Trudeau.

speechtext:
That was back in 1964. At that time we heard from a Canadian who, theoretically and intellectually, identified with the problem he raised.
Lest anybody should mistake the concern of the party I represent and of other opposition parties regarding the unemployment problems of Canada, I should like to indicate the number of times that we have raised questions in the House since September 7 on the economic problems facing the nation. These have nothing to do with agriculture, nothing to do with regional development, nothing to do with fisheries and local problems. They had all to do with the national, economic problems facing the nation. For instance, on September 27 we asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his colleagues 23 questions on this subject. On September 8 there were 12 questions, right on this subject. On September 13 there were 26; on September 16, the day of the release of the highly unfavourable unemployment statitistics, there were 32 questions, for a total of 320 questions. That is the number of questions that have been asked from September 7 until the present-the figures include questions asked yesterday-on the economic problems facing the nation. If I had time, and I do not, I should have liked to catalogue all the displays of callousness that have come from the mouths of the Prime Minister and his colleagues in responding to these questions. We have had deceit; we have had distortion; we have had concealment; we have had pretence; we have had hypocrisy and insensitivity; we have had confusion and we have had pious fraud, as far as I am concerned, and deliberate deception on the part of the Prime Minister and his colleagues regarding this matter.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT PROGRAMS TO STIMULATE THE ECONOMY - SUGGESTED NEW MEASURES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT PROGRAMS TO STIMULATE THE ECONOMY - SUGGESTED NEW MEASURES
speechtext:
That is what we were given in response to 320 questions that we asked on economic problems facing all Canadians, and especially the half million people who are presently unemployed.
On September 16 a number of questions were asked about the hard core unemployed. The Prime Minister used that term, we did not. He seemed to be the one who identified with it. I am, of course, referring to the 106,000 people who have been unemployed for more than six months and who make up over 20 per cent of the total number of the unemployed. Let me read what the Prime Minister said when asked about what the government intended to do to help these people. As reported at page 7867 of Hansard, he said:
-I believe the hon. member is referring to the hard-core unemployed and my understanding is that their number has decreased rather significantly in the past month.
I should like to say that, if you take the "hard core unemployed" compared to all those who are unem-
Alleged Failure to Stimulate Economy
ployeed, there has been a considerable increase in the number of hard core unemployed in the past four months.
Second, if the Prime Minister wants to present facts, let him give facts on unemployment as published by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics in 1971. We can see that for the past year there has been a considerable increase in the number of hard core unemployed and in the number of Canadians unemployed. If you want to go back for five years the figures would be lower. The Prime Minister tried to decieve the Canadian people by saying that we had had a reduction in the number of unemployed. I do not doubt for a moment that if you allowed him to bring in his own statistics, he could prove that to be the case. Nevertheless, on September 16 questions were asked about the astounding increase in the unemployment figures for the month of August, the largest increase in that month since 1946. The Prime Minister's response, as reported at page 7864 was:
There has been the biggest surge in job creation ever in the spring and summer months, and this has translated itself into a lowering of the unemployment figures for people 25 years old and over.
Having heard the remarks of the man I should like to be able to trust, I looked at the statistics and learned, for example, that if one compares the figures for 1970 and 1971, one will see that there has been an actual decrease in in the number of people over 25 years of age in the labour force of one-half of one per cent on a seasonally adjusted basis. In other words, people over 25 during the period the Prime Minister was referring to were actually withdrawing from the labour force. Clearly, there must be a tremendous amount of hidden unemployment that never shows up in statistics. In the period in question, that is, between August, 1970 and the same month in 1971, the increase in employment among those people was only one-fifth of one percentage point on a seasonally adjusted basis. I think statisticians will agree that is hardly statistically significant.
I could quote more of what the Prime Minister said regarding unemployment among young people. On the sixteenth we raised questions about unemployment, and the Prime Minister suggested that there has been a cut in unemployment and that the only problem was among young people; that was where the unemployment situation was the most grave. I believe, in responding to a question by the hon. member for York South, he said that he was referring to the fact that unemployment has increased because of the "participation"-that is the word he used-of young people in the work force during the month of August. On that basis he is taking his consolation. In response to a general question on September 16, he said and I quote:
Therefore the addition in the figures is caused essentially, I would say, only by the people in the 14 to 24 age group. This is obviously very serious, but the cause of it is not too well known. What we do know is that the rate of participation has increased; in other words, the number of people who at this time of year usually withdraw from the labour force have not withdrawn in that age group. We want to see the causes and reasons for that before being able to prescribe remedies.
In answer to a similar question on September 20, the Prime Minister said and I quote:
The problem is with the teenage group which has entered the
8310

September 30, 1971
Alleged Failure to Stimulate Economy
work force, or which has not left the work force after the summer period, at a vastly different rate from the past.
It is the teenage group. There is a tremendous amount of confusion. On the one hand, the Prime Minister does not admit the problem of unemployment. On the other, he says it is because of increased participation of the younger people in the labour force. He indicated it is the teenagers between 16 and 19 years of age. I can only conclude one of two things. Either the Prime Minister is deliberately trying to convey to the Canadian people some misconception of the whole problem or he is not aware of the fact that ever since the 1940's economists and demographers, or whatever these people who talk about Canada's growth are called, have been saying that the Canadian population will continue to expand through the period of the 1970s.
Everyone in Canada with any knowledge of the economy or of the population has been aware of this. I can only conclude that there must have been absolute ignorance if the Prime Minister has only now discovered we have an expanding labour force. Perhaps it is related to some of his domestic concerns or perhaps it is a deliberate attempt to deceive the Canadian people. The Liberal party can make up its mind which one it wants to choose.
When in Regina last year, the Prime Minister made reference to our expanding labour force. On December 3, as quoted in Hansard, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) made reference to the fact that we have an expanding labour force. In 1964, when we were beginning to get a recurrence of the unemployment problem, the then Prime Minister took consolation in the fact that we had an expanding labour force. In addition to these statements, people connected with the Economic Council of Canada, economists and Canadians from all walks of life, recommended that the government accept the fact that we have an expanding labour force and adopt immediate expansionary policies in order to remedy that problem. I challenge members opposite to deny that fact.
Anyone knowledgeable of the Canadian economy knows that the traditional economic models that can be applied to countries such as Italy, the Scandinavian countries or Britain, which have a relatively static labour force, cannot be applied to Canada. All Canadian economists recognize that when you have an expanding labour force you must have an economy which is growing, developing and expanding. How contradictory it is that in the past two years the government has insisted on cooling off the economy, cutting production, discouraging investors and discouraging initiative on the part of individuals, businessmen and, in fact, the whole business community, while at the same time recognizing that we have a growing country and a massively growing labour force. This can only be the result of absolute autocratic arrogance on the part of the people calling the shots.
The Prime Minister's office, the supergroup, autocrats, inner cabinet or whatever they are called, have shown tremendous arrogance. They know better than other parties, the Canadian people, the business community, labour people and economists. They are so damned pig-headed that they feel they know this or else they are ignoring what are the realities of the situation. Because of their intellectual seclusion, long years in universities reading books, and theorizing through Cite Libre, they are not aware of the realities of our country.

I wish to quote from the September 1969 Economic Council of Canada Perspective, 1975:
-the existing high rates of unemployment among young Canadians not only represent a waste of some of our most valuable human resources and a potential source of social instability, but also partly reflect a failure on the part of our society to bring young people quickly and effectively into active participation in the economic life of our country.
Dr. Haviland, a senior economist with the Economic Council of Canada, stated at the beginning of 1970 that we must have a real growth in Canada of 5.25 per cent a year just to keep the unemployment figures at their present rate, in other words to avoid having the unemployment problem grow worse. In 1970, the gross national product rose by only 3.3 per cent.
Another director of the Economic Council of Canada, Dr. Sylvia Ostry, stated in a detailed statement to the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, the same chamber which made a number of recommendations to the Prime Minister which have been rejected, that we need 2.6 million new jobs in Canada during the 1970s. Are we going to get 2.6 million new jobs with the kind of policies being advocated by the Prime Minister of this country?

I referred briefly to the proposed federal-provincial conference. Even learned members of the press were deceived when the Prime Minister first made reference to this federal-provincial conference. Day after day he has referred to the conference. He is trying to give the impression to the Canadian people that this conference on unemployment is the result of his own initiative. The hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald) placed that in proper perspective today. Day after day we have recommended an early conference specifically directed toward unemployment. The suggestion came, I believe, from Premier Davis of Ontario last year at the Victoria conference. The Prime Minister is trying to suggest that it is through his initiative that the conference will be held. This is absolute deceit, distortion, concealment and deception on the part of the Prime Minister of this nation. I hope that the Canadian people see what he is trying to do by misrepresenting the facts.
I wish I had a half hour to review some of the things we have recommended. In the 320 questions we have raised in this House, there have been numerous suggestions of a positive nature. Some of these were repeated today by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis). Not one suggestion that we have made has received a sympathetic or even polite response from the Prime Minister. We have recommended immediate tax cuts, not tax cuts such as those contained in the tax package which has been almost a decade in the making. We recommended immediate tax cuts for the low and middle income groups; selective corporate tax cuts and the elimination of the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials, which my colleagues will also recommend. Because of the inability of the govern-
September 30, 1971

ment to forecast the unemployment problem with any accuracy, we recommended an economic forecasting unit. That has been sloughed off discouragingly and disparagingly by the Prime Minister. He also recommended a sort of band-aid approach to the problems of this winter. We recognize that you cannot get programs with long term effects off the drawing board and into active operation within a matter of days or weeks.
We have recommended the introduction of a winter works program and other similar approaches intended to keep people off welfare and allow them to continue their normal way of living during the coming winter. The hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) has recommended special assistance to industries which find themselves in difficulty, through tax incentives, direct financing and the like. We have recommended to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Lang), who rarely appears in the House during debates on this subject, the removal of the three-year work experience clause governing the retraining programs of his department. We have recommended a consistent effort, together with industry, to end the system under which employees have to wait until lay-offs are announced before they can take advantage of industrial training programs. Many of these recommendations have had the support of the Economic Council of Canada. We have made numerous suggestions in the fields of housing and anti-pollution. If I had another 20 minutes or so at my disposal, I could develop the logic and reasoning behind many of these proposals, especially those which relate to tax cuts.
The frustration which is felt by members who are concerned about unemployed Canadians is mounting daily in the House of Commons because we cannot get the Prime Minister to recognize that a problem exists. I am sure this frustration is felt by members of the Liberal party as well as by members on this side. Unemployment goes against the life style of the Prime Minister. How can you be a swinger, how can you be happy-go-lucky, how can you do your own thing, travel all over the world and so on, yet be concerned about the little people who are unemployed? How can you be an elegant Prime Minister and at the same time be concerned about those who are unemployed, living in small rented apartments in Hamilton, Toronto and Halifax?
Of all the recommendations we have made, there is only one I should like to put forward now, in conclusion. It is that the Prime Minister, at the earliest opportunity, give the people a chance to replace him as the head of the government in order to bring some sensitivity and concern back into Canadian politics.

Alleged Failure to Stimulate Economy
He has tried to convey the false impression to this House and to the Canadian people that the economy of our country is in deep trouble, an impression which is totally denied by the facts. He has tried to suggest that the substantial proportion of Canadian trade with the United States is somehow the result of the failure of government policies. The reality is that the high proportion of our trade with the United States is a very obvious and completely natural consequence of the fact that our country has had the good fortune to border on the richest market in the world. I am sure most Canadians are well aware, even if the NDP is not, that this factor has contributed substantially to our achievement of a very high standard of living.
In striving to gain political fortune from adversity, however, the leading Cassandra of the NDP has never allowed himself to be deterred by realities, and if adversity does not exist he seeks to invent it. Every difficulty he seeks to blow up into a calamity.
During the opening debate on second reading of the Employment Support Bill, when Parliament reconvened earlier this month, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) pointed out that virtually every major indicator provided clear evidence that the Canadian economy had been expanding at a steadily accelerating rate for almost a full year.

During the first half of this year, the nation's real output of goods and services rose at an annual rate of 6.2 per cent, which was almost double the growth during 1970 as a whole. I can see why the hon. member for Prince Edward Hastings (Mr. Hees) disdains statistics, too. They just don't support his attitude. During the second quarter of this year, the real gross national product rose at an annual rate of 8.9 per cent, which was the largest quarterly increase in two years.

Total capital investment rose by 5.7 per cent during the second quarter and business capital expenditures by 6 per cent.
Although the expansion has been steadily gathering momentum over a period of several months, I do not mean to suggest for a moment that we should relax or that there is not room for further progress, particularly in the creation of new jobs and faster progress in bringing down unemployment.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT PROGRAMS TO STIMULATE THE ECONOMY - SUGGESTED NEW MEASURES
speechtext:
As the minister told the House in his speech on September 7, a number of the new economic measures announced by President Nixon in mid-August obviously pose a serious threat to the strong growth under way in our own economy.
The upturn which has occurred in the rate of price increases this year is a further matter for concern even though it is due in no small measure to a rebound in food prices after the decline last year resulting from the supermarket price war.
As I said a moment ago, we are deeply concerned about the high level of unemployment. Despite the simplistic approach from members of the opposition, this is a complex problem. The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that as a result of the steady expansion of the economy over the past year there has been a big increase in the number of Canadians with jobs. In August of this year there were a quarter of a million more people employed than a year ago. This increase of 3 per cent in Canadian employment during the 12-month period was more than three times the increase in employment in the United States during the same period and outstrips the performance of all other industrial countries. This performance is all the more impressive when it is recalled that during the early stages of rapid economic expansion a large proportion of the increases in output comes from the higher production of workers already on the job, rather than through employment of new workers.
Hon. members should know that unemployment among adults has declined over the past several months. The seasonally-adjusted rate of unemployment among those 20 years of age and over, who make up 86 per cent of the labour force, has dropped from a peak of 5.9 per cent in July, 1970, to 5.3 per cent in August of this year. In the case of men and women 25 years of age and over, who make up 70 per cent of the labour force and include most of the heads of households, the seasonally-adjusted rate of unemployment declined from a peak in July, 1970 of 5.2 per cent to 4.4 per cent last month. While I certainly do not regard these rates of unemployment among the more mature members of the labour force as being satisfactory, they do indicate that substantial progress has been made in alleviating the problem in this important and largest sector of the labour force.
In increasing measure, the core of our unemployment problem in Canada has come to be focused on youths 14 to 19. And even here the source of the problem does not stem from a slow growth in employment. In August of this year, employment of youths 14 to 19 was actually 50,000 higher than in the same month last year. This represented an extraordinary year to year increase in the number of teenagers with jobs of some 5 per cent. The source of the unemployment problem among teenagers results from a phenomenal increase in the number of these young Canadians who have entered the labour market in search of work. Let me hasten to point out, particularly for the benefit of the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Lundrigan), that I am not talking here about the increase that has taken place in the total number of Canadians among the population aged 14 to 19. That increase is, as the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) has asserted,
quite predictable. What has never been predictable, and has always been subject to wide variation, is the number of youths 14 to 19 who will enter the labour market to seek jobs at any particular time.
This point is perfectly illustrated by the developments of the past year. During the 12-month period ending in August, the total number of Canadians aged 14 to 19 increased by 2.4 per cent. But the number of boys and girls in this age group who entered the labour force increased by 6.3 per cent, which is about triple the increase in the population of this age group. Because even this increase in jobs was not sufficient to absorb the still larger rise in teenagers seeking work, there was an increase in the numbers of this group without work last month on a seasonally adjusted basis. This increase was the sole cause of the rise in seasonally adjusted unemployment for all workers in August. It should be evident that the very sharp jump in the number of teenagers recorded by Statistics Canada as being in the labour market, and the associated degree of unemployment among this group, presents a rather special problem which will have to be attacked in a special way. As indicated to the House previously, the government is focusing on this question urgently in order fully to understand it and to deal with it effectively.
In the motion which he presented to this House, the leader of the New Democratic Party chose to paint a stark picture of a stagnating economy and rising unemployment. He chose to ignore the fact, evident to most informed Canadians, that economic growth has been accelerating over a period of several quarters, and that the problem of unemployment as it affects our mature labour force is declining. Under the circumstances it is not surprising that he also chose to ignore the very substantial fiscal and monetary stimulus which we have given to the economy. In these circumstances, the massive nature of his specific suggestions for increased expenditures and tax reductions will not be seen by the Canadian people as anything but irresponsible. But then, Mr. Speaker, in this House the hon. gentleman has always been in the happy position of being able to advocate extreme courses of action without having to take the responsibility for the consequences. I recognize that within his party he has found it necessary on occasion to resist the still more extremist "wafflers" in his midst.
There is in the motion before the House the suggestion that tax cuts should be implemented. I point out there is a bill before the House that does propose to implement tax cuts as of January 1 next, and we are hoping that it will be through the House by January 1. Under the tax reform measure, every married taxpayer whose income is derived from salary or wages will pay less income tax. Every single taxpayer in similar circumstances will pay less tax if his income is under $8,000. Every retired taxpayer aged between 65 and 69 inclusive will pay less tax, whether single or married. Every retired taxpayer over 70 will pay less tax under the new system than under the old system if he is married, and less tax as a single taxpayer if his income is less than $8,500.
In addition to that, the prospect is held out in the tax bill of progressive reductions in the marginal rate of personal income taxes on the first $500 of taxable income from 17 per cent to 6 per cent, and a reduction of the general

September 30, 1971

corporate tax rate from 50 per cent to 46 per cent by 1976. All of these tax cuts are in legislative form and we do hope that we will be able to get them through the House in time for the people of Canada who want them to enjoy them. Perhaps members of the opposition are getting messages from their constituents different from those received by members on this side, but at least we understand very clearly that the people want these tax cuts.
The hon. member for Gander-Twillingate searched Votes and Proceedings and Hansard to find how many questions had been asked on general economic subjects by members of the opposition since the House resumed on September 7. I, too, searched Votes and Proceedings this morning for the same period to see how expeditious has been the work of this House. Leaving aside the previous opposition day as well as this one, on the 16 days of government business that the House has sat since resuming after the summer recess the opposition has "co-operated" in helping the House get its work done by moving no fewer than seven motions to adjourn the House under Standing Order 26; three motions to adjourn the debate, each of which required a recorded vote and consumed something between half an hour and one hour; two motions to adjourn the House, each of which also required a recorded vote and consumed between half an hour and an hour of time.
On the other hand, the government has on three occasions attempted under Standing Order 6(5)(a) to extend the sitting of the House in order that business might be proceeded with expeditiously and so that time that has been wasted by hon. members opposite in procedural manoeuvrings might be made up, to the benefit of the people of Canada. On each of those occasions more than ten members of the official opposition and New Democratic Party have stood in their places to frustrate the work of the House.

When I read the portion of the motion condemning the government for its failure to reduce Canada's dependence on a single market, I could not help recalling the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett's ill-fated attempt to blast his way into the markets of the world. It also brought back to mind the stillborn attempt to bring about a 15 per cent diversion of trade from the United States to Britain promised by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker)
Allged Failure to Stimulate Economy
when he was Prime Minister. Can the leader of the New Democratic Party do no more than seek to revive these abortive Tory efforts?
The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that we have worked very strenuously over a number of years to open up markets for Canadian goods and services wherever they were to be found around the world. I do not recall that in the past that approach has brought much complaint from the NDP. We have participated actively in international discussions to bring about a multilateral reduction of tariff and other trade barriers. We have a large trade service to help Canadian producers take advantage of every potential opportunity for new and expanding trade around the globe.
While there has been a substantial increase in the volume of our trade with other countries, the proportion of our trade With the United States remains very high. Is the Leader of the New Democratic Party-and I hope his predecessor in office who is the only member of his party in the House at this time will convey to him my comments-seriously suggesting that we should have discouraged Canadian producers from seeking to sell their goods in the largest, richest market in the world right on our doorstep, a market very similar in character to our own? Is he suggesting that we should not have entered into special bilateral arrangements with the United States, such as the auto pact and the defence production sharing arrangement, which have enormously increased our exports to the United States market? If that is the case, I hope he will have the courage to make his stand clear to the labour movement, whose friend he claims to be.
The government is aware, as the Minister of Finance suggested to the House a few weeks ago, that we will have to give consideration to the nature of our trade and industrial policies if the protectionist measures announced by President Nixon last month prove to be part of a fundamental change in the direction of United States policy and a move towards restrictionism. It would be very regrettable if that were to be the case. The government believes that, given access on reasonable terms, Canadian producers could look to the United States to continue to provide a rich and growing market for our industries. All Canadians would be the poorer if our entry into that market should become restricted for any prolonged period of time, and that applies to restrictions imposed by the United States or restrictions gratuitously imposed in Canada in the form of such ridiculous suggestions as export taxes on some of our resources.
As the minister has made clear previously, we are of course deeply concerned about both the short and longterm threat to our economy that is raised by the new policies announced by the United States administration. Only two days ago this House gave approval to an important measure to minimize the immediate adverse effect on production and employment in Canada resulting from the imposition of the surcharge.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion before us is of vital importance for the future of our economy. In listening to the speeches delivered up to now, we have come to realize that hon. members have a special concern for unemployment and inflaton problems.
The motion is of a very general nature, but in the few minutes that I am allowed I should like to deal very briefly with the causes of this deplorable situation and show that the government is not taking the appropriate means to correct it.
It is a recognized fact that this government's economic policy has brought disaster to Canada. As a matter of fact, everyone knows that unemployment is there. Figures are quoted, but nobody agrees on them, so much so that the Montreal newspaper La Presse published an article entitled "Statistics are, it is said, lies under scientific cover". If this is true, the fact remains that thousands of Canadians are unemployed, although they would like to

participate in the development of our country and to make an honourable living.
A former minister of the present government, the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer), resigned precisely because he could not agree with this government's economic policy. He did not share the government's views as to the necessity of fighting inflation. He, and various other experts, proposed changes, just as we, Creditistes, have been suggesting extensive economic reform for a long time. Nobody listens to us much, but our principles are being adopted little by little, and I hope that eventually this solution-which, surely, is not asking for the moon- will be resorted to. It would not be heaven on earth, but it would at least solve many problems.
If our economic system was really good, it would give satisfactory results. A bad tree cannot bear good fruits. Our economic system has very good points, but it also has bad ones. We have to keep what is good and correct what is bad. What are the effects of our economic system? General displeasure. Let us discuss with people on the street, in service stations, in stores. We do not even have to question them. We only have to ask them: "How are you?" At first, they say that everything is fine. After a few minutes, we hear them say: "Well, I have a problem. I do not work. My business is in poor condition. The operations of my plant have been slackening".
People are complaining about the bad condition of our economic system which contributes to create inflation, unemployment, bankruptcies and disorder.
This government taxes people more and this increases the cost of living. Why does it tax? The financing system of the public sector is forcing this government to get us more into debt from one year to the other. One has but to read the annual statistics for Canada to realize that, year after year, our country, which is supposed to get wealthier, is getting deeper and deeper into debt. In order to pay for interest on this ever-growing debt, this government has to levy taxes from Canadians. We have reached the point where we are paying more than $2 billion a year in interest on the public debt.
Mr. Speaker, with $2 billion we could achieve great things in order to solve the problems that we are now facing. The increase in interest rates is a direct factor of inflation. Inflation is the main cause of the increase in the cost of living. These are related. Inflation does paralyze the economic sector of construction. All contractors say: "We are building less because we simply cannot borrow money at a reasonable rate". Since they are unable to borrow at a reasonable rate, they slow down their operations and hire fewer workers.
Inflation is a disincentive for businessmen with the result that numerous projects are postponed indefinitely. I talked with smart businessmen in several regions of Canada and they told me that they were postponing their projects because interest rates were too high and that decent profits were out of the question.
Even governments, especially the federal government, will not proceed with public works because of inflation. There are many requests for buildings and post offices to be erected in various Canadian municipalities, but pro-
September 30, 1971

jects are being paralyzed for want of money and because of inflation. Many problems for Canadians stem from inflation. Extension and construction projects for hospitals and some institutions are at a standstill and this is felt even in Montmagny where a heavy increase in unemployment is foreseen for the coming months due to the anticipated shutdown of the Chemcell plant.
This is why, Mr. Speaker, I ask the federal government to reimburse to the province of Quebec the millions of dollars collected by means of the so-called social development tax. With these sums, the Quebec government surely could pursue construction of public buildings such as hospitals, homes for retarded children and senior citizens; this could alleviate unemployment and increase the workers' purchasing power.
Unemployment stems from inflation. Unemployment erodes the over-all purchasing power of Canadians, which in turn dampens consumption of goods. A decrease in consumption creates overproduction, which then leads to a slowdown in the operations and often the shutting down or bankruptcy of industries.
Bankruptcies, while they may at times enrich some people, nevertheless impoverish many more. Victims are businessmen, traders, workers and the number of bankruptcies is constantly increasing. Businessmen are therefore concerned with this situation.
Recently, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce held a convention and the former president, speaking of government interference in the field of enterprise by way of taxation, of unduly high taxes which paralyze enterprise and hinder its development, expressed the following views:
The speaker also dwelt on the ubiquity, the meddling and interfering of federal and provincial governments in the Canadian economy.
It is the duty of business leaders, he said, to initiate more energetic action if they wish to prevent new legislation from putting an end to their operations.
They are already beginning to stir in their sleep. They need a lot of time to wake up. They must be shaken very hard to voice their fear in public. They are concerned about the future of their business.
I quote further:
Never in the past has the ability of Canadian businessmen to run their business in an efficient way, to develop it, to make a profit and to be competitive been so severely challenged by the labyrinth of laws.
To conclude he said this:
Many businessmen will give up and all the clever young people who could have been attracted will stay away from business.
Mr. Speaker, that is a very serious note of alarm that Parliament ought to take into account if it really wants to find valid solutions before it is too late.
I shall say only a few words about agriculture because we often have the opportunity to talk about it. In that area, producers are concerned about the situation.
Most farmers are in a plight. Hog producers for instance are having extremely hard times. Costs for electricity, telephone, feed, transportation, building materials and chemical fertilizers keep rising, adding to production costs. On the other hand, prices paid for hogs are clearly too low.
Alleged Failure to Stimulate Economy
I was recently visiting a hog producer in my riding and he told me that it costs $11.50 to breed an 8- to 10-week-old piglet, while he cannot sell it for more than $8 or $9. Obviously it means that he suffers a loss instead of making a profit. Those who sell carcasses on the market are not having any better treatment and their income is insufficient.
Egg producers are not in a more enviable position because it costs 36 cents to produce a dozen eggs, and the average price is 30.8 cents a dozen. Therefore, from the standpoint of income these producers are hardly any better of than the unemployed, and yet they are compelled to work hard every day.
The motion of censure suggests that the government undertake winter works. In my opinion, these as well as summer works should be undertaken because it is cheaper to carry out water, sewage and road projects in summer than in winter.
There is much work to be done in almost all municipalities but these are in no position to go ahead owing to the high cost of the price of money.
So in April the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities submitted to the Canadian government a brief from which I would like to quote a few extracts so as to draw the government's attention on the merits of this resolution. I quote:
WHEREAS the difficulties and high cost of borrowing is one of the principal impediments to municipal capital financing, and WHEREAS there is mounting need for investment in such urban development programs as: urban transporation (including the acquisition of land for right of way), housing, pollution control, water supply, recreation facilities, industrial sites; and WHEREAS it is not in the national interest for our municipal governments to be obliged to compete with federal and/or provincial governments and private corporations in the capital market; BE IT RESOLVED that the Federal and Provincial Governments be asked to undertake, after consultation with the municipal associations, the establishment of a specialized municipal credit institution or institutions to facilitate municipal borrowing for capital works.
It ends up saying:
We ask as well how the Federal Government can extend interest free lending privileges to underdeveloped nations while refusing to extend those same privileges to underprivileged municipalities that are so numerous in Canada.
There, Mr. Speaker, is a resolution which should not only be carefully considered, but applied so that we may immediately help municipalities achieve their projects.
There was no alternative: we had to suggest that the government use the Bank of Canada to finance the public sector, or build public works which would help give jobs to the workers and increase the total purchasing power of the consumers. Public works add to the wealth of the people in that sense that they can use public property. In addition, as I have just pointed out, they increase the total purchasing power.
Sometimes we are told: That is not possible. So, why try to use an institution to this or that end? Mr. Speaker, I can tell you that the great Liberal leader, Mr. Mackenzie King, on September 23, 1935, in Saskatoon, at a time when there was an electoral campaign to be won, knew that the

September 30, 1971

people were aware of the situation. In fact, he said, and I quote an editorial:
The Liberal party believes that credit is a public matter which does not only concern the bankers-
I also agree with this-
-Capital flow should be related to the domestic social and industrial needs of the Canadian people.
That was true in 1935, and it is true now in 1971. He was very severe when he said, quote:
Once a nation loses control over its currency and its credit, it does not matter much who in that nation makes laws. Once in control, money lenders will ruin any country.
We are being lead to ruin-
-As long as control over currency and credit has not been restored to the government and acknowledged as being its most obvious and most sacred responsibility, any talk of democracy and Parliament supremacy is vain and futile.
We have ample proof of this: Parliament falls far short of supremacy, because it has to submit to the whims of high finance, which dominates the Canadian economy.
The Right Hon. Mackenzie King also stated, I quote:
If my party is re-elected, we will assert our monetary policy in the greatest battle between high finance and the people ever witnessed by Canada.
The great battle announced by Mackenzie King never took place. As a consequence, and because of a series of acts of treason, we are now close to ruin-
Mr. Speaker, I would say in conclusion that changes should be brought about in order to allow the whole population to reach a reasonable standard of living and the guaranteed annual income, which is possible in Canada. All there is to do is simply use the remaining crumbs of our rich resources.
If that is not done, I think we will be guilty of a great treason as a great economist once said and I quote:
He who strips someone of his clothes will be called a thief; and he who does not cover a naked man when he can do it, is he worthy of another name?
The Holy Scriptures contain a part which should make us think. Being Christians, we have the right to take our inspiration from them. There was a rich man and at his gates laid a beggar. All the beggar wanted was the crumbs which feel from the rich man's table, but the latter kept turning him down. And it came to pass that both died. But they were carried to different places: the rich man was in hell and saw Abraham afar off and Lazarus in his bosom. And he cried and said: "Father Abraham, send Lazarus that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am tormented in this flame". But Abraham said: "Son, remember that in your lifetime you received the good things and likewise Lazarus the evil things. Now, he is comforted and beside all this, between him and you, there is a great gulf fixed: so that he which would pass from hence to you cannot; neither can you pass to him, that would come from thence".
In these circumstances, one could derive pleasure from this situation. But I am serious when I say this. I mean that if we do not take the steps required to assure a minimum guaranteed income for each Canadian, destitution will continue to increase; it will widen the gap between men and contribute to enrich those who hold the credit monopoly and who can use it for their own pur-

poses, by refusing morsels to the less fortunate. The day will come when this destitution will give rise to agitation among the people, but it will be too late.
It is essential to work together to assure a minimum income to each Canadian citizen and we will thus have done our duty.

We on this side of the House believe we are in a crisis, but those on the other side believe we are only approaching it. As I listened to the parliamentary secretary telling us how good things are in Canada, I wondered whether he was aware of the latest report in the Ottawa Journal. I want to put it on record because it deals with lay-offs. It will show that the parliamentary secretary is definitely in a dream world if he thinks things are good, particularly when we look at the results of this government's fiscal

and monetary policies and its strategy in the fight against inflation. We see a frightening picture, and I do not use these words lightly. It reveals a stagnant economy, regardless of what is said, with an intolerable rate of unemployment and business failures.
It can be quickly concluded that all these matters spell disaster for the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his government, and a tragedy for Canada and Canadians. Confidence in the economy is now absent, or at best a rarity. How can our quality of life be improved without that confidence? How can we reach full employment without that confidence and how can we reach full productivity? There is an alarming and ever-growing concern being registered by people from all walks of life and in every segment of our society regarding the frightening and bleak economic future of Canada.

A cross-Canada survey by the Canadian Press shows lay-offs- some permanent, some temporary-hitting a wide spectrum of industries.
No industry appears immune because of size alone. Some layoffs involve 2,000 workers.
Let me put on the record figures in respect of the lay-offs about which we are talking to show that these do not hit just the large urban centres but small rural areas as well. How can the parliamentary secretary stand in his place and talk about this country being in such great shape? That should be beneath his dignity. To those who are employed, unemployment means reduced prospects for advancement and promotion. As a result of massive unemployment industries stagnate, and so do the prospects of those still working. For those not in the work force, such as students, wives, mothers and young people, massive unemployment reduces or eliminates the prospects of these people getting jobs once they enter the work force. Accordingly, Canada adds these groups to the unemployment rolls and loses the benefit of utilizing their talents and skills.
For the elderly and the poor, unemployment means increased hardships and/or premature retirement. An economy riven with unemployment has no capacity to increase its treatment of the marginal worker. Massive unemployment is the tip of an economic iceberg, and it causes our economy to suffer an irretrievable loss in output and income. I should like to repeat that the greatest asset of this country is its human resource and it is terrible to see that we have so many employable people who are not able to obtain employment as a result of the fiscal and monetary policies of this government. Alleged Failure to Stimulate Economy
opposition day is designed for the making of constructive suggestions by the opposition. Without question, we face difficult circumstances. Without question this problem is one of agonizing, personal dimensions for those people affected. The problem, obviously, has been compounded by recent events in the United States. There is the 10 per cent surcharge, the proposed job development credit plan which is now before the American Congress and, even more ominous than that, the proposal for "Domestic International Sales Corporations", or the DISC proposal.
All these compound the problem which we are all aware of and pose, I suggest, serious threats to employment levels in this country. Therefore, given this situation, the opposition could at least address itself to the sort of adjustments it would expect the government to undertake. One would expect that opposition suggestions would be responsible and precise, and that there would not be an insistence on a response to hypothetical problems. May I say that some of the suggestions made recently as to what we ought to do in the event of the DISC proposal going through Congress are not serious or responsible.
