speechtext:
The hon. member is asking what the government is going to do. The government has taken steps. I am going to deal with them. The hon. member has been in this House longer than I. He should know that proposals are not announced on an opposition day. These sort of gratuitous comments are not in keeping with the hon. member's understanding of the purpose of opposition days.
I now wish to deal with the specific motion before us. The first proposal is for a "large scale program". In his speech, the hon. member for York South made no mention of the dimension of that scale. He did not attach any money figure. He made a grandiose suggestion at a time when we face serious and precise problems.
8320

September 30, 1971
Alleged Failure to Stimulate Economy
The second proposal is for an immediate reduction of taxes. Everyone in this House and the Canadian public know that there is a tax bill before this House which, by all predictions, is not likely to get through this House until some time in November because members want to debate it at length. This bill makes precise proposals dealing with tax reductions such as higher exemptions for senior citizens, the elimination of the 3 per cent surtax on personal income and a whole series of proposals dealing with employment expense allowances which would permit wage and salary earners to deduct 3 per cent of their income up to $150 a year. Also, child care expenses will be deductible up to $500 per child up to 14 years of age with a maximum of $2,000 per family. Some of these proposals also deal with deferment of transportation costs for members of the labour force who move from one part of the country to the other.
The set of proposals will take one million people off the tax roll, reduce taxes for 4,700,000 and generally accomplish the purpose outlined in this particular motion. No mention was made of this. No mention was made of the fact that the government is behind these tax adjustments and would like to get them through as quickly as possible. We believe the Canadian people are also behind them.
The third proposal deals with forcing down interest rates. This is also a general and attractive statement. No precision is attached to it. I will deal with interest rates for a second. As the hon. member for York South knows, in recent years there has been an expansionary monetary policy which has had a lowering effect on interest rates. What has been the effect? The most important effect has been that short term interest rates are at their lowest levels since the early 1960's. For example, the yield from 91 day Government of Canada Treasury Bills in last week's auction was 3.98 per cent. A year ago the yield was 5.61 per cent. Yields on 90 day finance papers have been in the range of 3.25 to 4.5 per cent a year, also substantially lower than levels in recent years. It is somewhat irresponsible to frame a strongly worded motion such as this and not say anything about what the interest rates should be. This is just a general statement about interest rates.
The approach taken by the New Democratic Party in this debate can only be described, and I am trying to be as generous as possible, as opportunistic and irresponsible. They know the government's record. How much further would they go? If they are talking about a fund for municipalities, how much money are they talking about? If they are talking about interest rates, how much lower should they be? The leader of the New Democratic Party did not say a single word on those points. He simply presented a broad set of proposals, all of which are attractive. He has not made any precise suggestions. I do not see how these proposals can be treated as other than opportunistic, irresponsible and a systematic attempt to play with a very serious and agonizing problem.
I now come to the fourth proposal. The Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Andras), a very competent minister, will be dealing with housing matters. The motion suggests large additional funds for housing. This is another grandiose statement, undisputably attractive. The opposition knows the government's record. They know the budget for housing this year is something like $942 million. If they are serious about this, how many more

million are they talking about? Why has the leader of the New Democratic Party not enough intellectual honesty and political courage to define precisely what he means by this rather grab-bag omnibus motion? He did not say a word about details. I again dismiss this as a general and attractive statement. It again is opportunistic and irresponsible because it fails to go beyond what the government has done in precise terms. Our budget is $942 million. We are aiming at 220,000 new housing starts this year. The government has paid particular attention to providing money for low income housing. Where does the New Democratic Party stand on this particular question? We have not heard a word about that. It has been dismissed in a way which is not worthy of the hon. member for York South. We did not hear a word about the $200 million that has been designated for experimentation and innovation to provide housing for low income families. There was no recognition of this imaginative proposal, not a word.
The fifth suggestion deals with money for waste treatment plants. In the past 10 years this government has spent $432 million to assist municipalities and others to build waste treatment plants. If the hon. member for York South is serious, and I hope he is, how much is he talking about? If this amount is inadequate, how much more would he put into it and from where would he draw the money? Would he increase taxes or shift money from other government programs and, if so, which program? Until we get these precise answers from that party, we can legitimately accuse them of being opportunistic and irresponsible for introducing a motion such as this.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT PROGRAMS TO STIMULATE THE ECONOMY - SUGGESTED NEW MEASURES
speechtext: The sixth suggestion talks about redirecting trade from the U.S.A. I find this particularly galling. The speech by the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Lundrigan) was of the type that we expect from him. I have studiously avoided dealing with it. It was replete with unattractive adjectives and offensive. It was the type of speech which opposition members have often made containing snide, critical comments about trips abroad by ministers. No person has been subjected to more snide and critical comments than the Prime Minister. We know and the opposition know that the trip to the Soviet Union and the trip to countries in Asia were primarily designed to deal with expanding and diversifying our markets. They know that perfectly well. They have made snide comments about those trips, taken political advantage and exploited them. Yet they have the unmitigated gall to come before this House and, as part of an omnibus resolution, ask us to take steps to diversify our trade. This is an indication of the degree of integrity embodied in a motion before the House today. Let me deal with the trade question.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT PROGRAMS TO STIMULATE THE ECONOMY - SUGGESTED NEW MEASURES
speechtext: Let's hear you.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT PROGRAMS TO STIMULATE THE ECONOMY - SUGGESTED NEW MEASURES
speechtext:
The hon. member says "Let's hear you", and I shall be delighted to oblige him. Over the past decade, that is, from 1960 to 1970, total Canadian exports have increased from $5.4 billion to $16.9 billion, an expansion which is more than threefold. Exports to overseas
September 30, 1971

markets, that is, to markets excluding the United States market with which the hon. members opposite are so concerned, increased from $2.35 billion to $5.9 billions, or by 250 per cent. Exports to the United States have increased from $3 billion to $11 billion, an increase of 350 per cent. Among the major industrial countries, the most rapid growth in Canada's trade has been with Japan. Exports to that market have increased by 450 per cent. These are the facts. Yet the motion refers to the introduction of a program designed to protect Canada's future by redirecting trade so that it will not continue to be at the mercy of a single market.
As I say, trade with Japan has increased by 450 per cent. The hon. member for York South knows this to be the case, or, at least, ought to know it. But no mention of this aspect was made by him. Exports of manufactured products now comprise nearly two-fifths of our total exports as compared with 12 per cent a decade ago. The preponderant proportion of this increase has been in exports to the United States. Highly manufactured products now comprise about one-half of Canada's total exports to the United States, and the United States now absorbs about 85 per cent of Canada's exports of highly manufactured products. Again, the hon. member for York South knows this. I would have thought that since the new economic policy of the ited States is presently, in part, before Congress for consideration the House would have heard some suggestions from the New Democratic Party as to what Canada's posture should be. It would be helpful, not only to the Canadian people but helpful generally if it were recognized that there were some risks and difficulties attached to trade in any export market. They are not peculiar to trade with the United States. It could be that in future we will encounter similar difficulties with respect to, say, Japan, or the German market. We support the idea of diversification. Achievement in this area has been part of the government's record. But it is important to recognize that diversification alone would not eliminate the risks which are essentially involved in the export business.
I wish to deal with the situation as it is today, with special reference to the final point made in the resolution before the House. The implementation of recent United States measures, particularly the surcharge and the investment tax credit feature has introduced a disruptive element in the development of north-south trade in manufactured products. The Canadian government has remonstrated strongly against the application of these measures to Canada, not only in terms of damage to Canadian industries but also in terms of basic United States selfinterest. If it should turn out that these measures reflect a new and continuing intention on the part of the United States to frustrate the development in Canada of a mature and balanced structure, then clearly Canada must adapt to such a circumstance.
I do not believe we should respond to these measures until there is a much clearer indication that they will be approved by Congress. To me, it seems a symptom of the obsession in the minds of members of the New Democratic Party that they should ask the government to declare what its position would be in the event of a measure going through Congress. It seems to me that a mature party would not give way to an obsession of that kind. Yet this is
Alleged Failure to Stimulate Economy
the approach opposition members are taking. In support of the general attitude being taken by the government, let me quote from a speech made by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) in Houston, Texas, yesterday:
If we were now to find that United States policies were turning inward and that the United States considers it as in their interest to import our raw materials and our energy resources but to impede and obstruct the development of our secondary industries, we would have to take a very hard look at our whole economic relationship with the U.S. Indeed, in that case, we would need to fundamentally reassess our own trade and industrial policies. It would be an "agonizing reappraisal".
It would, indeed. We should not for one moment minimize the importance of United States trade. If the hon. member for York South had some single scheme in mind whereby Canadian trade could be directed away from the United States without producing the most serious consequences for Canada I should be glad to hear it. He should come to my riding, and I will get some of my steel workers to talk to him about the realities of the situation.

speechtext:
I turn to the speech made by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner). He began by saying that every member of this House was concerned about unemployment. When I intervened to say that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was not, he chided me and suggested I was not telling the truth. Let me remind the parliamentary secretary that some 18 months ago, when the Prime Minister was attempting to deal with the inflation which was facing this country, he said he would not be deterred from pursuing his antiinflationary policies even if the country had to face unemployment at the rate of 6 per cent. Well, the rate is now 6 i per cent. I say, as I did when I interjected, that the Prime Minister does not give a damn about unemployment. The statement which the Prime Minister made was a heartless, unfeeling and uncaring statement by a man of wealth who never had to think about what it means to be unemployed, a man who, when he thinks of unemployment if he thinks of it at all, does so in terms of the kind of statistical gobbledygook we have been getting from ministers in this House.
The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) was here a few minutes ago. Before he came here he was president of the National Federation of Trade Unions. He understands the significance of the recent announcements of lay-offs by Domtar and Alcan. He must know, because he led these men in the strike at the end of which they gained recognition in 1941. The present Minis-

September 30, 1971
Alleged Failure to Stimulate Economy
ter of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) knows what it means for a person who has been employed at relatively high wages to find himself out of work with payments due on a mortgage, or on an automobile or on a television set. He understands the uncertainty they face when they are laid off without knowing when, if ever, they are to be called back to work. Working people caught in a situation like that can look forward only to living on unemployment insurance until that runs out, and then going on welfare. Those other ministers I have mentioned may be concerned, but the Prime Minister has never been concerned about the unemployed. We have heard all kinds of rationalization. We have been told that the participation rate in the labour force is higher now. We have been told that the situation has improved, but that suddenly and unexpectedly there has been a sharp increase in the number of young people unemployed.
The facts are crystal clear. We need not take the word of Members of Parliament, or academic economists, or labour economists, or business economists: Statistics Canada gives us the figures each month. What do these figures show? For 16 months we have not had a seasonally adjusted unemployment rate of less than 6 per cent. The government can squirm and argue, but nevertheless this is the fact and it cannot be wished away. In August 1971, we had 455,000 people unemployed, an increase of
7.000	over August 1970. This was the month before President Nixon announced his new economic policies which, according to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin), will mean that if these policies are continued for a year there will be an extra 90,000 people unemployed.
We have been told that with the exception of unemployment among young people things are better. Just what is the situation as far as these young people are concerned? In August 1970, among the age group 14 to 24 there were
217.000	unemployed. In August 1971, there were 240,000 young people unemployed, an increase over the previous year of more than 10 per cent. We have been told that long term unemployment is getting better. If it were not unparliamentary, I would say that statement was a lie. Let me give the House the facts. In August 1970, there were 79,000 people in Canada who had been unemployed for more than six months. In August 1971, there were 106,000 people who had been unemployed for more than six months. Is this an indication that the situation is getting better? To me it indicates an increase in the number of these unemployed of 25 per cent or more.
We have also been told that the participation rate has improved. You can do anything with figures, Mr. Speaker, but at least this statement is true. In August 1970, the participation in the labour force was 57.9 per cent. In August 1971, it was 58.1 per cent, or 0.2 per cent better. These are the real facts and government ministers, and parliamentary secretaries who would like to be ministers, can argue all they want. The fact is that we have not done enough for the unemployed. One would think that by some accident, that through some act of God, Canada has the largest unemployment rate of any industrial country in the western world. That is not an accident; it results from deliberate government policy. I pointed out earlier

that when the Prime Minister inaugurated his anti-inflation policy he said that even a rate of 6 per cent unemployment would not deter him from his policy of restraint. Well, we have that amount of unemployment. In addition, this year we have a rapidly rising increase in the cost of living.
On the same day the unemployment figures for August were published, the Globe and Mail carried an article headlined "Cost of living, jobless rate up". I have said something about the jobless rate, and let me put on the record what this article had to say about the cost of living:
Official statistics on jobs and prices in Canada showed yesterday that high unemployment has stubbornly resisted the loosened economic policies that have permitted a new upsurge in the cost of living.
The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate rose in August to 6.5 per cent of the labour force. It was 6.3 per cent in July, slightly below the 6.4 rate for June.
At the same time, the cost of living went up 0.7 per cent, following a 0.8 per cent increase in July, pushing the total increase for the 12 months from August, 1970, to 3.4 per cent.
More than two-thirds of this rate of 3.4 per cent is attributable to the latter half of the year and the early months of 1971. We are now experiencing an increase in the cost of living at an annual rate of 5 per cent or more. I am simply saying that the government's policy regarding full employment has been a failure. The government's policy to combat rising costs has similarly been a failure. We have the worst of both possible worlds.
This afternoon we have had the same sort of speeches from the "juniors", the would-be ministers, the parliamentary secretaries, that we have had for a couple of years from the big chiefs.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT PROGRAMS TO STIMULATE THE ECONOMY - SUGGESTED NEW MEASURES
speechtext: And you keep ignoring what we say.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT PROGRAMS TO STIMULATE THE ECONOMY - SUGGESTED NEW MEASURES
speechtext:
Let me put on the record a couple of the gems. The Prime Minister said on March 18 last in this House that the government had taken a series of steps intended to alter the course of the economic policy, but that some time must elapse before those steps could be fully productive. Then, he continued by saying he thought that all the economic indicators showed that the economy was moving. At the time the Prime Minister made that statement in March, 1971 we had an unemployment rate, seasonally adjusted, of 6.2 per cent. Six months later, in August, the unemployment rate had risen to 6.5 per cent.
Then, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), who is always so optimistic, said on November 12, 1970, that he had recently publicly suggested that on a seasonal basis unemployment had about reached its peak, and he expressed confidence that we could look forward to continued improvement. At the time he made that speech in November, 1970 the seasonally adjusted rate of unemployment was 6.5 per cent. In August last, it was once more 6.5 per cent. Recently, the Minister of Finance said in this House, on September 7, in response to some comments made by the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), that unemployment would continue to decline. He challenged the Leader of the Opposition to resign his leadership if the predictions made by the Leader of the Opposition to the effect that unemployment this year would not go below 6 per cent did not materialize.
September 30, 1971

I challenge the Minister of Finance, who has made repeated speeches in the House as well as statements outside the House in which he claimed unemployment was going down and that things were getting better, to follow the suggestion he made to the Leader of the Official Opposition, and if unemployment does not drop in any month for the balance of this year below 6 per cent, seasonally adjusted, that he resign his position. I say this because if ever there was a minister who has given the people of this country bad advice, it is the Minister of Finance.
We had a new, novel and ingenious explanation by the Prime Minister a few days ago of why the rate of unemployment, according to latest figures, was 6.5 per cent. The Prime Minister said that things are better all round; that it is only among the age group 14 to 19 that things are worse, and that this was a completely unexpected development that no one knew about. Economists inside and outside the government service have been pointing to the very large number of young people, a product of the postwar baby boom, who would be entering the employment market during the next few years.One does not have to consult professional economists on this subject; I have a column written by Douglas Fisher in the Toronto Telegram for December 11, 1970, headlined "Unemployment hits young people". He is talking about the unemployment figures published for November, 1970 and the article reads:
The breakdown for November, however, showed an inordinate increase in unemployment among the 14- to 24-year olds. This is what the opposition focused on, not the slightly-dipped rate.
This was not something unexpected. The government had every reason to know that the number of young people looking for work would be much greater than had been the case in recent years. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) says we have not put forward any concrete proposals. Of course, that is not true, like most of his speech.

speechtext: The resolution we have put forward is pretty specific. It is as specific as any resolution can be in outlining the kind of program we think is necessary. We have gone into detail month after month in speech after speech concerning what is to be done. Last February the Premier of Manitoba showed his concern about unemployment, as the Prime Minister has not done. He announced a provincial program to meet unemployment, in so far as it could be done by the provincial government, in the province of Manitoba. I made a number of speeches in which I placed on the record the specific kind of thing the government of Manitoba is proposing. Let me summarize again for the parliamentary secretary, who said we were not specific, what the Premier said last February and what he proposed last week for the province of Manitoba.

I say that the government in Ottawa ought to follow the specific kind of proposals the government of
Alleged Failure to Stimulate Economy
Manitoba has already produced. Then I will tell you what we say.
I heard someone just say the Premier of Manitoba is going off to Europe. That comes with ill-grace from a member of a cabinet which has done more travelling around than any other. The Premier of Manitoba made clear that the trip he proposed to make to Europe would be postponed or cancelled if the Prime Minister should call a conference when he would have been away. He will be at that conference next week, next month or any time the Prime Minister calls it. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) knows this.
What the government of Manitoba proposed last February, and implemented, was a program providing $70 million for public works' projects and an expanded housing program. The province of Manitoba spent $110 million in capital works. That is what the government of Manitoba did. The parliamentary secretary asks what we would propose, specifically. I will tell him what we propose specifically, but I say that this country is entitled to, and can have, full employment. It is the responsibility of any federal government to be, if necessary, the employer of last resort. The federal government has the responsibility of seeing that people are put back to work.

speechtext:
No. I have no more time than the parliamentary secretary. I say the federal government should inaugurate a program of putting 250,000 people to work for the four winter months. Who are those people? I am thinking particularly of people in Peterborough, Hamilton, Montreal and Quebec City who have been unemployed for so long. They are unemployed and their unemployment insurance benefits have run out. I am thinking particularly of the young people who have not worked long enough to qualify for benefit.
I say we ought to find work for 250,000 people. How can . we do it? I suggest the federal government should grant to the provinces and municipalities $250 million toward capital costs in order that the municipalities and provinces may build things which are necessary and which are not make-work programs. To do that we have calculated it would involve a wage bill of $500 million. I am suggesting that half of that $500 million, in other words $250 million, be paid by the municipalities and provinces and that the other half be provided by the federal government in the form of long-term, low-interest loans.
Need I tell the Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State that 250,000 jobs provided in this way would have a dramatic effect in cutting back welfare costs which are beginning to strangle the municipalities of this country, including Peterborough. Need I remind the parliamentary secretary that 250,000 jobs would have a tremendous multiplier effect. He wants some specifics. I suggest to him that he remember and recreate a program begun by a Liberal government, if I remember correctly, under the then minister responsible for housing, now President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen).
I refer to a program which subsidized the building of houses in the winter by the payment of $500 per unit. Such a program would have a very dramatic effect in increas-

September 30, 1971
Alleged Failure to Stimulate Economy
ing house building and construction this winter, and Lord knows we need it. That is the kind of specific program I have been talking about. It is common knowledge in Ottawa that the government will not just let things go. Even if the Prime Minister has no heart, he wants to be re-elected, so there will be a program. What will it be? It will be another program of job training.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will not surprise anybody by taking part in this debate since there is in the opposition motion a reference to housing. There is a simplistic reference to it. Even if we accept the bald assertion in this motion that the economic policies of the government have produced massive unemployment, which I certainly do not, I do not think the House accepts that one of the simplistic solutions is captured in these few words of the motion, "large additional funds for housing". That phrase certainly has a nice ring to it. Who would not, least of all a minister responsible for housing, call for large additional housing funds? But I think in the very best of circumstances this somewhat self-righteous and overly simplistic generalization hides and distorts what this government has done and is doing for housing in Canada.
Of course, we are always considering the provision of more funds for housing. I hope that if and when we do inject more funds into housing, it will be done with full recognition of the complexities of the housing market. I will say now that I hope we never subscribe to the idea that this is totally an economic regulator and thereby withdraw funds from housing for limited objectives, nor will we simply force-feed funds into housing solely to reduce unemployment.
What we do, what we have done and what I hope we will continue to do is to achieve the basic housing goals of this country and at the same time seek to maximize employment benefits generated by residential construction. Certainly that will be apparent in the 1972 program which will be announced in this House in due course. It will take into account the twin objectives of the government, housing and employment.
I think, also, that we would be very wise to recognize that the residential construction industry is now operating at its highest level in Canadian history. NHA insured mortgage loans approved during the first eight months of this year exceeded the volume for any previous full year in the history of the National Housing Act.

I would say that this is a highly significant achievement. I think it is fully reflected in the actual 12 months' housing starts measured month by month from January, 1971, which at that time stood at 191,800, to a steadily increasing level in April of 203,800, in June to 220,400, and a further increase in July to 225,200. As of the end of August the actual starts in the previous 12 months were 230,000, which is by far the biggest record of housing starts this country has seen. I repeat that those are actual starts for the previous 12 months, and not forecasts. Speaking of forecasts, I would remind hon. members of the figures for August, which show that we were at the seasonally annually adjusted rate of 243,000. I think that heralds the continuance of a high performance during the winter, a performance of which we are not ashamed.
There is also reference in the resolution to this subject. In our CMHC sewage-treatment program, our achievement since 1968-69 is very real indeed. Federal outlays in
1968	for sewage-treatment facilities, loans to municipalities, were in the neighbourhood of $37 million. In 1969 they were $56 million and in 1970 well over $72 million. Indeed, in 1971 we will have committed $97 million.
I think these statistics reflect an upward and onward commitment to the housing and pollution control priorities of this government. The federal government's financial participation in housing since 1969 has increasingly been concentrated in the area of accommodation for those who cannot afford to obtain adequate shelter in the market. Here I refer to direct federal contribution. The
1969	capital budget of CMHC was set at $680 million, of which more than half, $359 million, was allocated for housing for low-income families and elderly people, while another $55 million was applied directly to accommodation for students. Of the balance, $170 million was devoted to direct CMHC loans to homeowners. This program began at that time to give special emphasis to the needs of those in lower-income brackets in areas outside urban centres where access to the private market was limited.
This activity in 1969 resulted in a commitment under the direct budget of CMHC which provided 27,470 dwelling units for low-income groups in that year. That trend was continued and expanded in 1970 when an unprecedented budget of $1,094 million was approved. It included several special programs. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) mentioned the $200 million innovative program, and there was an additional $240 million direct lending program inaugurated in late August of 1970. This year, 1971, again our direct CMHC investment in housing and related infrastructure will approach $1 billion. Of this amount, $789 million has been allocated to housing and virtually all of this sum is being utilized for housing for people in the lower half of the income scale.
I wish I had had the time to do more research and checking before coming to the House this afternoon. However, I think I remember when the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert)-who challenges me from time to time on housing-spoke in the standing committee which studied the CMHC estimates almost three years ago and said that the minister had better make a commitment to members of the House that he would invest at least $300 million a year in low-income housing from the CMHC budget. That figure was passed that year and we have
Alleged Failure to Stimulate Economy
more than doubled it every year since. There was no mention of that in any of the comments of the hon. member. I think the credibility of that party would have been much higher if this kind of fact had been placed before us along with their criticism.
All this means that in the three-year period 1969, 1970 and 1971 we will have produced 117,000 housing units for low-income people. In other words, more than one-quarter of all the housing that has been produced annually goes, by deliberate direction, to those whose needs are most urgent. In those three years we will have begun, in terms of housing starts, 50 per cent more housing units for low-income people than in all previous years under the National Housing Act.
We were assured, on the private side of operations, in my consultations with approved lenders late last year that there would be a high level of private lender support, and this has been realized.
Our approach to 1971 has been taken on the basis that if we are to deal effectively with the variety of housing problems in Canada, and even within particular communities, we must introduce a flexible program and a more flexible use of instruments available to us under NHA. In 1971 we have been trying to exercise the increased flexibility which we began under last year's $200 million innovative program. This year, the CMHC capital budget commitment for federal initiatives of that nature in fact amounted to $451 million. Close to $100 million was allocated for a new program of assisted home ownership. Here we are utilizing reduced interest rates and extended amortization to get down, in some cases, to people with incomes a little in excess of $3,000, for the first time in a long time letting them experience home ownership.
I must say that most provinces are continuing to cooperate. They are providing various forms of assistance to complement federal efforts. These vary from interest rebates to homeowner grants with which most hon. members are familiar. The major elements of this program include interest rates which are now down to 7-3/4 per cent, and extended amortization to 40 years if the lower interest rate is insufficient to bring monthly repayments within the financial capability of the purchaser. About a quarter of the funds to which I have referred were committed in the first nine months of the year. We anticipate that projects will move into the "start" stage at a faster rate in the weeks ahead, providing for continuing on-site activity for many months to come, the many critical months to which hon. members are referring, in the winter of 1971-72.
Within the $451 million we allocated another $100 million to support the activities of non-profit organizations building rental housing for low-income families and individuals at rents agreed in the contractual obligation that goes with such loans from CMHC. That includes the section 15, formerly section 16, activities of the Quebec Housing Corporation. This section is used mainly for the provision of housing for elderly persons, for the handicapped and other disadvantaged people. Here again some provinces, but not all, provide assistance through capital or operating grants, and in these remarks I must recognize the very valuable contributions made by church

September 30, 1971
Alleged Failure to Stimulate Economy
groups, service clubs, charitable organizations and many others who are co-operating with us.
For the first six months of this year our program of non-profit loans produced commitments for 1,085 units and an amount of more than $15 million for new construction. Many of the projects are moving into a position where starts can be effected in the later part of the year and will be very valuable in creating employment in the winter months.
As part of the section 15 activity we also arranged for close to $100 million to be used for projects in 28 centres across Canada using the proposal call technique. We did this on a considerably smaller scale in 1970 and were encouraged by the results. We are extending it this year to provide needed rental accommodation throughout the country. Close to 3,000 units and $41 million have been committed under this special program to date, which will provide for new accommodation in such centres as Vancouver, Regina, Moncton, Pointe Gatineau, Hamilton, Brantford, Toronto, Ottawa, Windsor, Halifax, Calgary, Sudbury, Winnipeg, North Bay and St. John's. I hear my hon. friend from Peterborough (Mr. Faulkner) interjecting, but I do not see the name of his town on the list. In addition to these special efforts there is the direct CMHC lending program under section 58, formerly section 40, and a number of initiative and development projects where we are attempting new approaches in such areas as rehabilitation of existing homes.
So, Mr. Speaker, when we take into account all the lending activity under the National Housing Act for new construction, for the first six months alone we are talking about more than 70,000 dwelling units and close to 7,000 hostel beds, for an investment of close to $1 billion with many more projects in train now approved. I think that as a result we will have a record housing accomplishment this year. I think we can predict with conviction that 1972 will be another year of high production, with the housebuilding industry fully engaged. I also think that our low-income housing achievement in the 1969-71 period, which I fully intend to see carried forward into 1972 and beyond, is most gratifying. We will continue to thrust for an increasing proportion of our housing production to go into this area. I think it will be one of the thrusts that will serve to keep the housebuilding industry alive and fully active in 1972.
Having set some of those facts on the record, I wish to refer to some of the comments made by my hon. friend on this side of the House, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State, who asked some very pertinent questions as to the precision of the recommendations made by the leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Lewis) and other speakers who used such fine phrases as "more funds for housing." I ask: How much more funds? Where will it come from? What programs will it displace? Where will it be placed, and what of the capacity of the industry?
All sorts of questions are left hanging in the air by hon. members opposite. These are questions that must be thrown right back at them. We will be delighted to receive constructive suggestions that go far beyond the superficial, in-favour-of-motherhood expressions contained in the motion before the House.

Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege to take the floor after that earth-shaking announcement by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). I thought he might have said something in another vein, but I suppose he is still trying to solve the unemployment problem in his own way before calling an election. I am pleased that the Prime Minister is in the House this evening. It was regrettable that government members who were present this afternoon had to take so much abuse from hon. members on this side, because I think we all appreciate that they are not responsible for the mess the country is in.
The Prime Minister and what I might term his little power group of three or four make decisions in this country while the bulk of the members on the government side have to take the abuse. Any admiration I may have for them in this regard would be the same kind of admiration I might have for a flock of sheep.

We would then see a group of unemployed Liberal Members of Parliament. I think it is time we put the present policies of the government to the test.
The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance, the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Mahoney), and the minister in charge of housing told us this afternoon how good things are. They referred to a lot of statistics in respect of housing and unemployment to show how good things are. As an hon. member to my left said, they gave us the old numbers game. But when you have been around here for a year or two you realize that statistics do not mean very much. They are adjusted seasonally and in any other way in order to make the picture look as rosy as one wants. I think it is safe to say that no one actually believes this government or any of its members.
Let me read part of a letter I received from a farmer in Kelfield, Saskatchewan, in which he complains about taking out a cash advance. It compares the announcement by the government with the legislation passed. He said he took out a $2,400 loan on the basis of a statement by Otto E. Lang as recorded in the July issue of the Prairie Grains Policy Progress Report. He took out a cash advance. I will

Mr. Speaker, the government of Canada recognizes that there is a debt due to the farmers of western Canada in the amount of $38.5 million.
Yet the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) stood blandly in front of the television cameras the other night and said that $60 million is owing under the Temporary Wheat Reserves provisions. speechtext:
Some discussions on bills in committee have had face-saving value. Last year, when discussing Bill C-176, the Standing Committee on Agriculture saved the Minister of Agriculture from himself. It saved him from making, I hesitate to use the word, a fool of himself. At any rate, it saved him from himself in front of the Canadian people. If that bill had not been examined carefully and had been allowed to go through, I submit that the Supreme Court ruling of last summer would have rendered the bill useless. We are talking about an international trade war now, and we are worried about it. Yet if that bill under the aegis of the Minister of Agriculture had gone through, it would have precipitated the greatest interprovincial trade war imaginable. The international situation would have been as nothing compared with what might have happened interprovincially.
Government supporters have given a glowing report of our economy. They have tried to make their points from the right kinds of statistics. I recall, looking over newspaper headlines of September and October, 1929, that there were glowing reports then, too. Everybody said the economy would advance. That was the big point everyone made. There may have been little paragraphs on the back pages which indicated otherwise. But government and officials were saying that everything was fine. The same thing is happening today. Certainly, what the government says bears no relation to fact and to what is going on in this country.
I know the government is genuinely worried about the state of the nation today, but look at their priorities three years ago. Then they could have done something to avert the situation that is upon us today. What were their priorities? One of them was language, another was the bedrooms of the nation. Day after day we asked the Prime Minister questions. He did not answer, he just shrugged. That is the fashion now; if you do not want to do anything or say anything, you just shrug.
Then there is this business of skiing. I think the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Faulkner) talked about the Prime Minister's trips and how necessary they are. I believe heads of state should get around and maintain relations with other countries-personal relations. It is this continual round of skiing events and the Prime Minister's participation in that type of activity when the economy and the country are going downhill that bothers people to whom I have talked. They are not bothered by his visiting other heads of state.
Anybody who has watched closely the reign of this Prime Minister must conclude that his policy has been to confuse and to divide. Look at what happened to the Post Office Department. When I first came to Parliament you could receive a letter from my constituency in two days. How long does it take now? It could take two days or two weeks. Look at what the white paper on tax reform has done to the country and you will understand why today there is no prosperity in the country. People have no faith in the government, they do not know what the government is about to do next and hence business is reluctant to invest because investment may come to nothing. I think businessmen prefer to invest in other countries or keep the money in their own pockets.
Look at our youth and you will see the policy of confusion at work. Only a few years ago our youth were being
September 30, 1971

told that business was bad, that they should "do their own thing" and that type of thing. Now the Prime Minister is saying to the youth of this nation that they should help business. He is telling them to go along with business and that it is necessary. That was not his message two or three years ago. Look at our present situation. It is the direct result of this policy of division and confusion. Whether there has been any point in the attempts to divide and confuse the nation we shall have to wait and see. Much has been said on the subject and according to some sources that policy may have been intentional.
Opinions on foreign ownership have continually been voiced in this House. This fact has been deplored many times by my friends to the left. Foreign ownership and capital coming into this country have been deplored in many speeches made in this House. It is not the matter of foreign capital that should bother Canadians. However, there is a situation we should seek to correct. It is the matter of foreign industry coming into Canada being financed by the Canadian banking system. Hon. members will recall the stir in the House created by the sale of Ryerson Press last spring. No Canadian firm would purchase it. An American firm purchased it and then borrowed 90 per cent of the purchase price from one of our chartered banks. If there are to be any consequential changes to improve the system, perhaps should begin by studying our Bank Act which was last revised in 1967 and should be revised again.
We must discontinue ranting and raving about the United States which, basically, is our friend. We should not have expected to receive preferential treatment when our ministers visited that country a short while ago. We have betrayed them, in their eyes. The United States is a fact of life on the North American continent that we cannot ignore. The only way, I am sure, we will have prosperity with this government is if they start printing money again which will make our currency even funnier than it is today.
Some time ago I looked through the Bank Act. I noticed with regard to deposit reserves that the ratio is something like 12 per cent on demand loans and 4 per cent on contract loans. Of course, this is averaged every month. The last time I inquired, the ratio was 6.12 per cent. With the deposits which the chartered banks in Canada now have, which I think amount to approximately $33 billion, they could issue credit of approximately $428 billion. Whether this monopoly to issue credit to this extent is realistic in terms of maximum benefit to Canadians is something that should be reviewed by the House.
In conclusion, until we have in power a government that will do something other than divide and confuse we will be in continual trouble.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to deal with the second part of the motion moved by the leader of this party, as follows:
-nor can this House tolerate any longer the government's failure
September 30, 1971

to implement policies to reduce Canada's dependence on a single market and to assure a strong and independent Canadian economy.
I am sure there is no need for me to enumerate to the House the catastrophic effects which would ensue if the United States continued the 10 per cent surcharge on imports and retreated into some of the protectionist devices which are at present being discussed in that country. I agree with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) when he says that if these policies are continued it will be disastrous for Canada. The estimate of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin), that it would mean a loss of at least 90,000 jobs in Canada, is probably too low.
It seems to me we must ask ourselves how we came to be in this predicament and what we can do to rectify it. We should begin by asking how we came to be in this very difficult situation. I suggest the reason Canada is more adversely affected by the United States recent action is because we have virtually become a United States economic colony. Ever since the end of World War II the Liberal party has been the advocate of economic integration with the United States. Whenever we attack the government for its continentalism we get the kind of hoary answer given to us this afternoon by the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Faulkner) who asked, "Do you not want us to trade with the United States?" or the statement of the minister who has just resumed his seat that it is only natural that we should trade with the United States.
No one quarrels with that. Of course we must trade with the United States because of our proximity. The late President Jack Kennedy, when he visited Ottawa some years ago, said of our two nations that "geography has made us neighbours and history has made us friends." But there is a great deal of difference between trading with a country and being owned and dominated by that country. There is a great deal of difference in the relations between neighbours and the relations between tenants and landlords.
Of course we support trade with the United States. But what has happened in the process of continentalism is that we have gradually been losing the capacity to make our own economic decisions in this country. It is not that the government has not been warned of the apparent dangers of allowing the economy to be dominated and manipulated by another country. When some of us have been making these statements over the years we have been attacked as being anti-American or Canadian nationalists. We have not been alone. Many newspapers in Canada, and other publications, such as the Toronto Star, the Financial Post, the Financial Times and MacLean's magazine have been speaking out on this subject for the last ten or 15 years.
People in the academic community have warned the government of what is likely to happen. As a matter of fact, a former Liberal Minister of Finance, Mr. Walter Gordon, tried valiantly in the years between 1962 and 1967 to do something about this growing encroachment by the United States corporate power on the Canadian economy. We know what happened to him.
In order to appease public concern, the Liberal government set up the royal commission headed by Professor Watkins. This commission reported in 1967, and nothing has been done. For the past two years the Minister of
Alleged Failure to Stimulate Economy
National Revenue (Mr. Gray) has been making a study of foreign ownership and now we understand he has made a report to the government. We are still waiting for some action. Even the Leader of the Liberal party in the province of Ontario, Robert Nixon, the other day in a public speech criticized the government and said it had been too slow in dealing with this crucial matter.
The fact is that the chickens have come home to roost, and the chickens look very much like vultures. The Globe and Mail said in an editorial today that Canada now is in the position of being like a branch plant arguing with head office. In a television interview the other day the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said he was surprised that the United Sates wants to make Canadians hewers of wood and drawers of water. He need not have been surprised. Like Rip Van Winkle, he has just awakened to the world of today. They have been making us hewers of wood and drawers of water for decades, particularly since the end of World War II.
Instead of being aware of the situation, the Prime Minister has poured ridicule again and again upon those who have expressed their concern about the growing control of the Canadian economy by foreign investors. He has referred to them as Canadian nationalists and superpatriots. If we take the trouble to make a survey of the Canadian economy we find that foreign control has now reached the stage of economic domination. I shall not go over again the long, depressing catalogue of what the results of foreign ownership and control have been. Most members are familiar with it. In the last ten years the book value of foreign capital invested in Canada has doubled in size. The foreign ownership of the manufacturing industry is now 60 per cent of its total assets. Tobacco, rubber, machinery, transport equipment, petroleum, coal products and chemicals are all virtually in foreign hands to the extent of anywhere from 70 per cent to over 90 per cent.
The number of takeovers by foreign-owned and foreign-controlled companies has been increasing since the end of World War II, and the rate of takeover has increased sharply in the last three years. In 1945 there were 20 mergers in Canada. For the last three years there have been about 200 mergers a year, which has resulted in increasing control by foreign investors. Foreign ownership and control in Canada is the highest of any other country in the modern industrial western society. Two-thirds of the total investment in resource-based industries is foreign-owned. Three-fifths of the investments in manufacturing is foreign investment and four-fifths of that investment is American.
The United States investment in this country is growing rapidly. From 1945 to 1967 it rose from $5 billion to $28 billion and is now in excess of $30 billion. In 1955, American investment in this country averaged $500 a year. It is now in the neighbourhood of three-quarters of a billion dollars per year. This is so not only in the field of investment but in the field of technology. Some 95 per cent of the patents issued in Canada are registered to foreign owners, and of these two-thirds are owned by U.S. residents. Of the list of 25 leading countries in the world, Canada is first in the percentage of patents that are

September 30, 1971
Alleged Failure to Stimulate Economy
foreign-owned and last in the percentage of patents which are owned by its own nationals.

speechtext: So what?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT PROGRAMS TO STIMULATE THE ECONOMY-SUGGESTED NEW MEASURES
speechtext:
The hon. member asks, "So what?" When patents are owned outside this country I ask my friend to stop and ask himself who he thinks controls the economic activities of our nation. Of directorships of firms which are 50 per cent or more foreign-owned, only 44 per cent are held by Canadian citizens. The result of all this is that the Canadian economy has become more vulnerable than that of any other country to changes in U.S. economic policies, and we have reduced our capacity to respond effectively to any actions taken by the U.S.
American investment has had two main thrusts. Their major concentration has been on resource industries. The subsidiaries set up in Canada are producing for the parent company. They are not seeking world markets, they are seeking to produce raw materials for their parent companies, supplies that can be cut back when they do not need them or when they find other sources. These are raw materials which are sold to the parent company at an agreed price, not the world market price, with the result that the profits are very small in Canada and the wages are 25 per cent to 30 per cent less than those paid in the U.S.
These subsidiaries have no incentive to process or fabricate their raw materials in Canada. That is why we have a large trade surplus with the U.S. and why we have between half a million and three-quarters of a million unemployed, because these extraction industries are capital-intensive and not labour-intensive. What we have been doing is exporting jobs by sending our raw materials to the U.S. and elsewhere to be processed and fabricated.
The second thrust has been to set up a branch plant economy in Canada which was designed largely to benefit from the Commonwealth preferential tariff. The result is that many of these companies are producing only for the Canadian, or at the very most the Commonwealth markets and have not been anxious to enter world markets in competition with their parent companies.
It is all very well for the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce to say that he is not against diversification. Of course he is not, and I compliment him on the efforts which he and his department have made to diversify Canadian trade. But to what extent can they be effective in diversifying Canadian trade when they do not control the decisions that are made with respect to diversifying trade? If the Canadian subsidiaries of American companies are prevented by their parent companies from energetically entering the world markets, then all the trips that the minister and his colleagues make to various parts of the world will not be effective in bringing about the kind of diversification which is necessary.
The result of this branch plant economy is that most of our research is being done now in the U.S. and most of the patents, as I have already pointed out, are held in the U.S. The crux of the matter is that ownership means the power to make the decision that affects the economic livelihood of the Canadian people. It means that if the demand at any time lessens, then of course it is the subsidiaries that will be cut back, not the parent companies. The economic

decisions affecting this nation are not made by Canadians. In the main they are being made by gigantic corporations in the United States, and they are not being made in the interests of Canadians. It is bad enough to be hewers of wood and drawers of water, but it is even worse when someone else decides how much wood you will hew and how much water you will be allowed to carry.

lapse into a state of lethargy. This crisis ought to teach us the lesson that we must begin in Canada to regain control of the Canadian economy. We must now begin to make our economy more diversified. We must begin to process more of our primary products in this country. The hon. member for Duvernay (Mr. Kierans) warned the government about this in a recent speech when he pointed out that the whole tax structure of this country has been designed to give special assistance to the extraction industries which are capital-intensive, rather than to the manufacturing industries which are labour-intensive.
As a deliberate government policy we should be encouraging industries which create jobs, producing goods that will give our people work and opening up new markets for the products of our industries. If we do that, Mr. Speaker, this country will be much less vulnerable and we will be able to provide employment for our growing labour force. There is no use in the government complaining that we have the fastest growing labour force in the world and therefore it is very difficult to provide jobs. We have been warning the government for ten years that a quarter of a million young people a year are entering the labour market. We must now gear our economy so that it will expand at a sufficiently rapid rate to provide jobs, not only for those who are now unemployed but for the hundreds of thousands of young people who are entering the labour market each year.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this evening I would like to touch on two points. The first is that I feel we need much more centralized economic planning, and the second concerns the youth unemployment problem. With respect to my suggestion that we need more centralized economic planning, it is my feeling that in the present situation we do not have enough planning at the centre and we do not have enough co-ordination among the many departments and agencies of government which produce economic effects.
There are a great many departments of government which do produce economic effects: for example, there is the Department of Finance, the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, the Department of Transport, the Department of Agriculture, the Department of the Environment, the Department of Manpower and Immigration, and the Treasury Board.
I suggest that we should have a minister whose primary concern would be the co-ordination of the economic policies of all these departments and the development of general economic policies. I suggest that we should have a minister of state for economic policy who would undertake this task. I understand that at the present time the job is being done by a committee of ministers, the principal member of which is the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) who is assisted by other ministers who have responsibilities in the area of our economy. I believe these ministers have other administrative concerns to occupy their time to the extent that they cannot concentrate
Alleged Failure to Stimulate Economy
primarily on developing economic policies both for the long-run and the short-run.
At present we have the Economic Council of Canada, but it has basically a long-term role. For short-term economic planning we have two branches within the Department of Finance, the economic programs branch and the economic analysis branch. I suggest that a minister of state for economic policy should have jurisdiction over these two branches, which should be taken out of the Department of Finance, and that such a minister should report to the House for the Economic Council of Canada in the same way as the Minister of State for housing reports for CMHC. He would also be in a position to submit problems and programs to the Economic Council for long-term study and analysis.

speechtext: Can I conclude from the hon. member's remarks that he no longer has confidence in the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) since he recommends a minister of state for economic policy?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT PROGRAMS TO STIMULATE THE ECONOMY-SUGGESTED NEW MEASURES
speechtext:
No, indeed. Mr. Speaker, I listened to several of the speeches made today. While I heard a great litany of the economic problems facing the country, I did not hear many positive suggestions to solve those problems. It is my impression that a debate like this should be one during which Members of Parliament put forward our ideas for discussion and consideration. Our ideas may not all be good, there may be shortcomings in them, but this is the place to express them.
One of the best speeches on economic policy that I heard in this House was made by the hon. member for Duvernay (Mr. Kierans), a former minister. His was one of the most thought-provoking speeches made to the House in a long time. But it seems that all the opposition do is think in terms of personalities.
I think we would be much better off if we could have our discussions on a policy level-but instead we hear the kind of remark just made by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath).
I said I intended to refer to two matters. My first point is that I think we need more co-ordination of our economic departments and a minister should be appointed whose prime concern is economic analysis and planning. The other matter I should like to deal with is youth unemployment; and I admit, as does the government, that this is a serious problem. The government has tried to develop a program to deal with the unemployment of youth. I would refer the House to the report of the Youth Committee entitled "It's Your Turn". I think this report has been much maligned. Unfortunately, the media has concentrated on two very minor aspects of the report, one dealing with the legalization of marijuana and the other with cadet training.
If one reads the report he will find that the principal concern of the Youth Committee was the problem of youth unemployment and most of its recommendations

September 30, 1971
Alleged Failure to Stimulate Economy
relate to a program and policy to solve this problem. It is unfortunate that the report has been maligned and criticized for matters which are not dealt with principally. The analysis of the youth unemployment problem in this report is excellent. At page 15 of the report, in the summarization of the youth unemployment problem the following is stated:
-Canadian youth experience a consistently high rate of unemployment, even when the economy is at or near full employment;
-the variations in youth unemployment during the business cycle exceed variations in all other groups in the labour force;
-the ratio of the youth unemployment rate to the national unemployment rate has increased during the latter part of the 1960s and reflects a general deterioration in their employment prospects;
-there are distinct regional differences in the employment opportunities for the young.
The report goes on to analyse the reason for this problem among our young people-which is growing worse each year-and states that without any relationship to the general level of our economy, even when our economy is good things are not good for our young people. Let me suggest to the government and the House that we must do more for our young people in the way of giving them training, but not merely at the university level. A few years ago it was part of the Liberal party platform that we provide young people with 100,000 scholarships. That program was replaced by the Canadian student Loans Plan, which is a good one. I suggest that we reconsider a national scholarship program, but let it be a scholarship program directed not only to young people going to university and college but young people going into trade school, going abroad to learn different trades, professions, or the arts, including music and similar skills.
The scholarships should also be used in conjunction with industry and commerce so that young people can be trained while on the job. This would work in a way similar to the apprenticeship training program of the past. If we look back to the 1920s and the 1930s we will remember the apprenticeship programs. In those days employers were willing to hire young people under the apprenticeship program for a period of four or five years, during which they received training in all aspects of commerce or the industry concerned. They did not pay very much but they were being trained while working. When they finished the training program they were in a position to accept and carry out work responsibilities, which many of our young people are not prepared to do today.
We should provide grants directly to industry, business or to the young people in conjunction with grants to industry and commerce, to promote this type of training. Perhaps this could be done through tax incentives, grants or scholarships, but I think it is essential that it be done. This would not only help our young people, it would help employment generally by keeping young people off the labour market for a few years and giving job opportunities to older people who are raising families.
Let me refer to another very good suggestion in the Youth Committee report. The suggestion refers to a Canadian youth employment directorate. This would be a special directorate to assist the Canadian government in resolving the problems of youth unemployment. One of the principal recommendations of the report appears at page 168 as follows:

Therefore the committee recommends that the federal government set up the Canadian Youth Employment Directorate (CYED) to take immediate action in the following areas: a) in the area of structural youth unemployment, given the high ratio of youth to adult unemployment and the variations in success at finding a job associated with region, socio-economic status and ethnicity,
i)	the CYED act as an interlocutor in all governmental social and economic development programs to ensure that the specific employment problems of youth are taken into consideration;
ii)	the directorate undertake extensive research into the nature of youth unemployment with a view towards defining and evaluating the range of alternatives for public action;
iii)	the directorate establish, if necessary, direct programming to create viable alternatives to present training and retraining programs-
The report also suggests that we reconsider the three-year delay we have in our manpower training program which prevents young people benefiting from these programs unless they have worked for three years. Our government and this House must take a close look at this recommendation. It is one that has been made by others.
I do not wish to take up much time of the House as I know other members wish to speak, but my principal purpose in intervening in the debate was to make these two points. I shall repeat them. We need more economic planning and co-ordination, and I suggest we should have a minister whose sole responsibility is directed toward this end. My second point is that we should pay much more attention to the Youth Committee report "It's Your Turn", especially those parts of it which relate to youth unemployment. I think it is a good report in that respect.

speechtext:
This government has shown, above all else, that it has no answer for any problem. The hon. member who spoke was quite right. He said there is not enough planning. My conclusion, having watched this government operating for three years, is that they do not plan at all. The cupboard is bare. It has been bare for three years. There are no plans and no alternatives. The government is bankrupt of ideas and of alternative programs for the people of Canada. Worse than that, the government does not even know what to do tomorrow. That is why today
September 30, 1971

we are not sure whether a federal election will be called next week, next month or next year.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT PROGRAMS TO STIMULATE THE ECONOMY-SUGGESTED NEW MEASURES
speechtext: The hon. member is coming closer all the time.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT PROGRAMS TO STIMULATE THE ECONOMY-SUGGESTED NEW MEASURES
speechtext:
They cannot make up their minds because they have no alternatives to place before the Canadian people. I have been a member of this House for some time and have watched governments operate. I have tried to appreciate the problems that cabinet ministers face, as well as some of the problems they encounter in running a country as large, diversified and complex as this. In 1957, when I first came to this House, the government I supported faced pretty serious problems it had not known about. There was the hidden report of 1957 that we did not know about. The Canadian people did not know about it either. The report told the government of the day that a recession was on the road and that we should prepare for it.
The previous government had not prepared for it. We had to prepare for it. We had to face the fact that there would be a recession, and there was a recession. We fought it by coming up with new, imaginative schemes for putting Canadians to work. We keep asking the present Prime Minister what programs and plans the government intends to bring forward to create jobs for people this winter. We are worried about unemployment. We know there will not be enough jobs around to keep employed all the people presently working. We want something to be done about this.
We did not do anything unique in 1957, but at least we did something. We employed people through the Department of Public Works. We made the Department of Public Works the main vehicle by which people were able to work during the winter months. We put many people to work. We improvised, I would say effectively, by producing a winter works program. We introduced the roads to resources program and considered the disadvantaged provinces, the prairie provinces. We brought out the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants under which we gave the governments of these regions more money which they could pump into the economy and thereby put more people to work.
These days members of the opposition direct questions at the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) day after day. They ask, "What are you going to do?" The Prime Minister says, "We will do something some day." We say to the Prime Minister, "You are running out of time; provincial governments are running out of time; municipalities are running out of time. If you do not tell them what you intend to do, how can they tie their programs to what you will do?"

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT PROGRAMS TO STIMULATE THE ECONOMY-SUGGESTED NEW MEASURES
speechtext: Absolutely right.

speechtext:
We want the government to produce a program that will provide jobs for people. That is what we are interested in today. We know, as the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) has said, that many people will not enjoy a merry Christmas on December 25 if this government continues in its ineffectual and ineffective way. All the government says is, "Well, maybe tomorrow we will have a program for the unemployed of Canada."
Alleged Failure to Stimulate Economy
I think we all like listening to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson). We wish he were right about the stories he tells, stories that he got from "Alice in Wonderland."

speechtext:
Although the Minister of Finance may look into the looking-glass, we do not know what to say to our own constituents about how they are to survive this winter. More important, we do not want to see a repetition this winter of the sort of half-baked, ill-conceived summer programs this government has produced. I am referring to programs such as Opportunities for Youth. Surely to goodness the government will not try to introduce for the unemployment this winter the same type of program that it introduced for our youth this summer. Surely to goodness there need not be the nutty, "weirdo" schemes that under the aegis of the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) were produced for students this summer. Those programs put into disrepute the government, the people involved and Members of Parliament.
It seems that the government is willing to gamble on anything in the hope of providing some sort of employment for somebody. That is what happened this summer and I do not think the members of this or any other opposition would be willing to go through that again. Yet we get nothing except lame and hair-brained excuses from the government. Perhaps part of the blame should be laid at the feet of members of the government. As I see it, Liberal Members of Parliament-this includes a great many members of the cabinet-have abdicated their responsibilities and allowed the growth of an oligarchy headed by the Prime Minister. He surrounds himself with people who are not elected, people like Marc Lalonde, Ivan Head and a great many more.

speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT PROGRAMS TO STIMULATE THE ECONOMY-SUGGESTED NEW MEASURES
