speechtext: We in the opposition have suggested to cabinet ministers that these fellows are really the ones who are in control. It is nice to know that the Prime Minister can bring out lists and say, "I am promoting this fellow, that fellow and some other fellow to the position of parliamentary secretary, and those who are left I will make ministers or chairmen of committees so that everybody in the Liberal party will have a position."

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT PROGRAMS TO STIMULATE THE ECONOMY-SUGGESTED NEW MEASURES
speechtext: That is shameful.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT PROGRAMS TO STIMULATE THE ECONOMY-SUGGESTED NEW MEASURES
speechtext:
The Prime Minister says, "Really, though, when it comes down to power and control, the technocrats in my office and around me run this country." That is the situation we have arrived at in this country. Elected representatives, excepting the very favoured few whom the Prime Minister likes, have nothing to do with governing this country. The rest of them sit by and condone and accept this situation because the pay cheque at the end of the month is bigger, because the Prime Minister has appointed them to this, that or the other position or acknowledged that they should be chairmen of this, that

September 30, 1971
Alleged Failure to Stimulate Economy
or the other committee, or ministers of state of this, that or the other department. But the technocrats have proven over three years that they do not have any answers to anything. They get large salaries, a lot of help and are well paid-and they know that we have a great deal of unemployment and lots of inflation.
It is time the Liberal party again took over the Liberal party and started producing some action and results. Let us look at a few facts-inflation, for example. We watched this government create unemployment, hardship and misery because they were fighting a great battle against inflation. What are the facts? The rate of increase in the consumer price index, January to August, 1971, is a little short of 5 per cent, 4.8 per cent to be exact. Last month there was a monthly increase in the consumer price index of no less than 7 per cent, or an annual rate of increase of 8.9 per cent. That is some battle! That is some victory! That is a pretty poor performance.
What about the Atlantic provinces? The Atlantic provinces are more adversely affected than at any other time in their history. The Prime Minister said that he was really going to look after regional economic disparity. The only way he has looked after it is by spreading it across the whole nation. That is not what we wanted to see. We wanted to see it eliminated, not spread. We do not want the cancer to go across Canada; we want to cut it out and eliminate it completely. But that is not the way it happened.
What about unemployment in the Atlantic region? Our people received really good news in August: they were told that 9.4 per cent of the people in the Atlantic provinces were unemployed! The same is true for July. In August, 1970, it was 8 per cent. It increased 1.4 per cent in one year. The sad fact is that the situation is no better in Quebec. Quebec keeps talking about separating. I do not know why we in the Atlantic provinces do not do the same. We face the same adversity as the people in Quebec.
What about Nova Scotia? We had a change in government in Nova Scotia. Things were going to be good with a Liberal government in Ottawa and a Liberal government in Nova Scotia. Oh boy, things were going to be good. This is how good things are in that province: in August, 1970, the rate of unemployment was 5.6 per cent. In August, 1971, it was 6.5 per cent, an increase of almost 1 per cent. The number of unemployed in Nova Scotia has increased from 14,000 to 19,000. The rate of unemployment has gone up from 5.1 per cent to 6.8 per cent.
We used to be proud of the fact that Nova Scotia had the lowest rate of unemployment in the Atlantic provinces. Now only Newfoundland exceeds us. If Nova Scotia continues with a Liberal government we will probably pass Newfoundland. I am sure we will pass them because in the very near future the clock will run out on the Premier of Newfoundland and there will be a Conservative government in the province. Things are bound to be better. They cannot be worse.

hoots like an owl. He only comes out at night. He never says anything. He is not a very wise owl. As a matter of fact, he is rather stupid. I have never heard him make a speech. If he ever does, I will be willing to come here and listen.

speechtext:
I wish to give an example of what is happening in my constituency. For 22 years we had an engineering office of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. It looks after many things for the three Atlantic provinces, in co-operation with the federal government. It has been there since the Maritime Marshland Rehabilitation Act was passed. It has been very effective and very valuable to the area. What does the present Department of Regional Economic Expansion intend to do? It is going to close this office. The department talks about bringing industry to the area, but it is going to close an office which contains more expertise and information than ever existed in any one body at any one time. Rather than try to keep these people working at a time of high unemployment, the department suddenly decides to lay off these 65 people. They are going to eliminate the problem of those 65 people being unemployed by putting them on welfare or unemployment insurance. That is the way they are going to correct the situation in the Atlantic provinces.
This government is bankrupt of ideas. It has been ever since it took office. They are a bunch of technocrats, most of them not elected, who are trying to run this country. The sooner we get rid of this government, the better the country will be.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT PROGRAMS TO STIMULATE THE ECONOMY-SUGGESTED NEW MEASURES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT PROGRAMS TO STIMULATE THE ECONOMY-SUGGESTED NEW MEASURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I had spoken earlier today I would have dealt with our position with regard to the United States, our industrial potential and our balance of payments, situation-but charity takes a little time and I do not have much time. It may appear that I am being rather ruthless with our party and the government tonight.
It is about time we got away from the state of shock into which we were thrown when the surcharge was announced by the President of the United States. It is understandable that for a time the surcharge will leave us a little shocked, not quite certain what we can do and hoping that it will disappear. The surcharge will disappear. We went to the United States. We asked for concessions. We did not get them. The newspapers said the surcharge might be lifted. Because all of these things might happen, I decided yesterday to go to Washington to find out whether we are going to be exempted or whether the surcharge is going to be lifted. I was told that I would never be able to get this information.
Mr. Speaker, I spoke to the highest officials and elected representatives in the committees of ways and means, finance, and rules. They laid out the whole program. There is no doubt in the world that the surcharge will be lifted. When? When the DISC program is passed, when the United States gets its own terms as far as world trade is concerned, as far as its economy is concerned and as far
September 30, 1971

as the monetary exchange situation is concerned. As far as Canada is concerned, they do not even know we exist.
One gentleman I spoke to in Washington said, "Mr. Otto, did you try to buy anything in Washington with Canadian money?" I said, "yes, I tried to buy something. The storekeeper who had been dealing with Canadians for 40 years looked at the money and said, I think this is Canadian money, isn't it? It is no good here'." I say without any rancour toward the United States that as far as they are concerned, we do not exist. They meant the surcharge to be applied against us. The DISC program is against us, everyone else is against us-and to hope that things will get better is absolute fallacy. This government has to come to the conclusion that this situation is with us. There are going to be no world trade agreements outside of a great favour by the United States. If they leave, they will leave in their favour. They admitted this. Kennedy is gone; the Kennedy program is gone. They are in a position where they must protect themselves against the onslaught of many other nations.
Let me deal with the DISC program. I wonder if Your Honour is aware of the awful results it might have for us. This program is designed, in brief, to set up a corporate tax haven in the United States for all export companies. Congressmen and Senators told me, "We know we have multinational corporations spread all around the world because they can get tax advantages by operating outside the United States. We cannot legislate to bring them back but we shall create a tax haven in the United States which will give them tax-free profits."
Mr. Speaker, there will be loopholes so wide that all the expenses can be charged against domestic production and all the profits counted against exports. No subsidiary company can possibly exist in Canada when the DISC program takes effect, unless they are out of their minds, because the advantages will be fantastic and every United States corporation which is responsible to shareholders will pull any of its subsidiaries right out. This will reduce our industrial potential by 20 per cent. This is a fact. I hope everyone will realize it is a fact because then we may be able to get on with a program without all these political repercussions, a program which will give us a chance to exist and to grow.
My time is running short, Mr. Speaker. I suggest that apart from pulling in subsidiaries, the United States move will result in an increased tendency among Canadians to invest in the United States. It is said it would mean a $100 million loss to the treasury, which is equivalent to $200 million profit by corporations, which is equivalent to about $3 billion in exports and, as the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) has said, since we do about 70 per cent of our import and export business with the United States most of that export portion will be thrown on Canada, so we are in double jeopardy.
The first essential is this: the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) must tell Canadians that we can be independent of the United States. We can be industrially and economically independent. Let us wash away all this supposition that we cannot do something because we are merely 22 million people. This is the first time in our history that we have a Prime Minister with such a great following among
Alleged Failure to Stimulate Economy
Canadians. They will listen to him. If he has confidence, and I think he has, he will say, "We must expand our export endeavours, increase our research activities and develop our independence along worth while lines."
I see the house leader for the NDP is making a sign as if to cut my throat. I gave him an undertaking that I would be very brief and I hereby stick to that undertaking. The task now falls upon the Prime Minister to tell Canadians that we can do great things, that there is a great destiny ahead of us if we only have the will, without the help of the nebulous United States which will disappear as far as we are concerned, anyway.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT PROGRAMS TO STIMULATE THE ECONOMY-SUGGESTED NEW MEASURES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for York East (Mr. Otto) for permitting one of our party to wind up the debate on our motion. I do not know that I can do much better than he was doing.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT PROGRAMS TO STIMULATE THE ECONOMY-SUGGESTED NEW MEASURES
speechtext: Maybe you should have let me finish.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT PROGRAMS TO STIMULATE THE ECONOMY-SUGGESTED NEW MEASURES
speechtext:
I did not prevent the hon. member from finishing. All I will say is this. The action taken by the United States in imposing a surcharge against Canadian goods is forcing us to reassess our position. There were members on the government side who sought to bring about such a reassessment in days not long gone by. Some of us remember Walter Gordon. He brought in a financial policy which was designed to enable the Canadian economy to become less dependent upon the United States, an economy which was viable and able to protect itself. All of us recall perfectly well what happened to Walter Gordon. Since then we have consistently followed a policy which has made the Canadian economy increasingly vulnerable in the kind of situation in which we now find ourselves.
The economic policy which the government has followed since I came to this House in 1968 has made us increasingly vulnerable to measures of the kind taken in the United States. It has sought to make the dollar increasingly expensive. The Canadian dollar has been protected, and those who own Canadian dollars have been protected. But the worker and the farmer have been made the fall guys. If I had 20 minutes in which to speak I would fill in the background. The government has sewn us up piece by piece, month by month. As the hon. member for York East said, it is now time for them to come up with some of the answers.
Mr. Speaker, they do not have the answers. They have placed the Canadian people and the western farmers in a vulnerable position. I could see this coming. Anyone could have seen it coming right from the time the United States refused to renew commodity agreements-the sugar agreement, the wheat agreement. Now we are standing out in the cold. At no time have members on the other side produced a policy which would enable the Canadian people to survive as a community and provide for themselves what they need to enjoy, well-being, jobs and security. We are waiting for the government to come up with solutions and quit shadow-boxing. There was an excellent cartoon in one of the papers not long ago on this very subject.

September 30, 1971

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-PROPOSED AMCHITKA NUCLEAR TEST-POSSIBLE REFERENCE BY CANADA TO UNITED NATIONS OR INTERNATIONAL COURT
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-PROPOSED AMCHITKA NUCLEAR TEST-POSSIBLE REFERENCE BY CANADA TO UNITED NATIONS OR INTERNATIONAL COURT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I anticipate that the reply to my remarks will come from the Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister (Mr. Danson), so may I take this occasion to congratulate that courtly and courteous gentleman on his reappointment and say how pleased I was to see him on the survivors' list.
On September 16 I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) whether he intended that the Canadian delegation would bring before the United Nations General Assembly the question of the proposed Amchitka nuclear blast or if consideration was being given to having the matter brought to the attention of the International Court. On several other occasions in the earlier part of this session I inquired of the government's intentions in reference to this matter.
The Prime Minister's statement that the United States had not accepted jurisdiction of the International Court was probably an unintentional exaggeration of the reservations made by the United States Senate at the time of the ratification of the United Nations charter, which of course embraces the International Court statute. The Connally amendment, which interposed a self-judging aspect on U.S. acceptance of court jurisdiction, was designed to give the United States the right to determine unilaterally whether a subject matter of litigation lies essentially within its domestic jurisdiction. This is not quite the same thing as a blanket non-acceptance of the court's jurisdiction.
There is insufficient time to discuss this important question of international law in this short debate, but it can be said that contemporary developments and concern for the universal environment, if I may call it that, have internationalized many aspects of national behaviour which were once regarded as purely domestic.
Since my question was asked, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) has made his contribution to the general debate at the United Nations and discussed the very serious question of nuclear explosions. There can be little doubt that there is grave risk in the escalation of nuclear testing. The nuclear family is growing and the number of tests is dangerous. There may be some argument about the degree of fall-out danger, but there can be

no doubt that the world is a little more polluted and the environment a little more poisoned after each detonation.
This is why there should be continuing, vigorous protest against proliferating tests. I well remember the minister to whom I was parliamentary secretary discussing nuclear tests at the United Nations. The Hon. Howard Green always made the Canadian case with great clarity and with directness. He used to say, "We are against nuclear tests-period". So I agree with what I am advised the present minister said the other day at the United Nations. Not having had a copy of his address I must be general in my appraisal.
I believe we must be relentless in pushing for this final stage of the ban on nuclear explosions. It would be magnificent if the United States, which has given leadership in so many areas, were to set the example in this case and abandon its proposed Amchitka test, the test of a five-megaton bomb, a project which could so gravely affect the environment in such a broad area of the world. The project is called "Cannikin" and I hope that the United States will "can the Cannikin".
So serious is the situation that the Environmental Protection Agency of the United States has allegedly declared the test to be too dangerous to carry out. I must use the word "allegedly" because the report is secret under the imprimatur of the White House. But what we do know is that both Houses of the United States Congress have passed a bill banning the test unless the President gives his direct approval of it. In the House of Representatives the vote was 377 to 9 in favour of the ban; in the Senate no opposition was recorded.
The soul-searching and anxiety within the United States itself should surely prompt Canada to do its utmost to oppose this and all nuclear tests by all powers, and to push for international agreement that this particularly dreadful aspect of our modern technology be relegated to the discard of disuse.
We were shocked and astounded that the Prime Minister has not yet contacted the President on this matter and I hope that every effort will be made to do so. Speeches at international assemblies are important, but all channels of communication must be used to this end. This country must watch closely and make every effort it can to see that no opportunity is left untended that can push toward internationalizing a ban on this heinous aspect of our modern civilization. So we will watch what our delegation does at the United Nations now that our participation in the General Assembly debate is over.

speakeroldname: Mr. Barnett J. Danson (Parliamentary Secretary to Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-PROPOSED AMCHITKA NUCLEAR TEST-POSSIBLE REFERENCE BY CANADA TO UNITED NATIONS OR INTERNATIONAL COURT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) for his very extravagant remarks. I believe he was as extravagant in calling me courtly as I would be if I called him portly, but I do appreciate the sentiments he expressed.
On the question of further representation to the United States concerning the Amchitka test, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) have both very recently informed the House that no decision had been taken at this time to make additional representation. The Canadian government acted very promptly as early as February 22 of this year to make known to the United States government in
September 30, 1971

unmistakable terms our serious concerns about the Amchitka test. The text of the note delivered on the instructions of the Secretary of State for External Affairs was tabled by him in the House on March 29, 1971. Further representations, of course, would not be ruled out if it were thought that Canadian views were not already appreciated.
In this case, however, there can be no doubt that the United States government knows our concerns very well indeed and that these will be taken into account when the final decision on whether to proceed with the test is made at the highest level. At the present moment, the situation is that President Nixon has not given the necessary approval for the test and there is room to hope that the United States will reconsider its plans, as Canada has already formally requested it to do.
Canada's position has been further strengthened by debate in this House, by questions such as this by the hon. member for Hillsborough and by virtual unanimity in this House in backing the government's stand in opposing these tests. I hope agreement will be reached among the House leaders so that we may proceed with a debate to express that unanimity this coming week.
Canada has been actively pursuing a ban on all underground nuclear weapons' tests for over two years now in the appropriate international forum, the Geneva Disarmament Committee, as well as in the last two General Assemblies. At the forthcoming General Assembly we shall again be registering our concerns about and opposition to all underground tests, including the proposed test at Amchitka, as well as continued tests in the atmosphere. These latter tests in fact represent a greater threat to the environment from radioactive fall-out than do underground tests carried out by the United States and the Soviet Union.
The Amchitka test question is, in one dimension, a bilateral problem between the United States and countries such as Canada and Japan which are particularly concerned about it. In the United Nations context, however, nuclear weapons testing is dealt with as a general international issue, involving as it does a very considerable amount of testing underground by both the two major nuclear powers and in the atmosphere by the two nuclear powers-China and France-that have not adhered to the partial test ban treaty of 1963. At the twenty-sixth General Assembly, Canada will therefore continue to work actively, along with like-minded nations, for the ending by agreement of all nuclear tests.

subsubtopic: BILINGUALISM AND BICULTURALISM- REPRESENTATIONS BY ETHNIC ORGANIZATIONS- POLICY STATEMENT ON COMMISSION RECOMMENDATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since my question to the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) on June 23, 1971, asking for information on the federal government's policy with respect to the recommendations of Volume 4 of the B and B Commission report, interested Canadians have been waiting with patient expectation for
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
a long-overdue policy announcement. The commission set up on July 19, 1963, was instructed to inquire into, among other things, the contribution made by the other ethnic groups to the cultural enrichment of Canada and the measures that should be taken to safeguard that contribution.
Since that time the commission heard many briefs from organizations and private citizens, and on October 23, 1969, it presented to the federal government a report entitled "Book Four, the Cultural Contributions of Other Ethnic Groups". This report was then studied by various ethnic organizations in Canada who later presented their observations in the form of briefs to the Secretary of State. For approximately one year after that no official statement from the federal government was heard until September 12, 1970, when the Secretary of State delivered a speech at the Canadian Conference of the Arts in Toronto. I might add that the text of that speech was widely publicized and was favourably received by ethnic organizations in Canada.
I wholeheartedly endorsed in my public speeches the declaration which the Secretary of State made in that address, especially when he stated:
When we speak of cultural pluralism, we are making a fundamental choice for Canada both now and for the future, for we are talking about the development in Canada of a multicultural society. Canada is not a melting pot, and the government is opposed to any measure aimed at assimilation. It encourages all initiatives which have as their object the promotion and dissemination, along side the two main cultures, English and French, all other cultural values.
At this time I should like to say that the report of the commission dealing with the cultural contribution of other ethnic groups is an interesting and historic document deserving the serious study especially of the federal and provincial governments. Of the 16 recommendations in this report, ten are the responsibility of the federal government. I should like to urge that recommendation No. 14 be implemented as soon as possible. It deals with financial assistance to cultural and research organizations whose objectives are to foster the arts and letters of cultural groups other than the British and French. Furthermore, there is a great need to assist the ethnic groups of Canada in collecting and preserving their documents in the Archives of Canada.
Although six other recommendations deal with the teaching of languages other than English and French and are the direct responsibility of provincial governments, I believe the federal government should assist at least by providing funds for the publishing of language and history textbooks. Official bilingualism at the federal level in no way precludes the promotion and protection of other languages at the various provincial levels if other ethnocultural groups form a large enough body in these provinces.
I believe that retention of a language is an important factor in the evolution, development and expansion of a culture. Therefore, if any encouragement can be given to the teaching of more languages in Canada, it is important that such encouragement be given. That this encouragement is important is without question. That it should be provided I think becomes clear after one reads the 655
8342

September 30, 1971
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
paragraphs in volume IV of the B and B commission's report. We all proclaim equality of opportunity as an aim of the western democratic civilization to which we are committed.
I should like to urge the Secretary or State to appeal to his colleagues in the government to do everything in their power to assist in the preservation and promotion of the various ethnic groups making up the fabric of Canadian society. I believe that these efforts are worthy of our support because they can be defended on a realistic assessment of Canada as it is today. The very premise to the uniqueness of our Canadian plurality is based on the association of various cultural components in our society.
Identity does not just happen but must arrive out of a healthy, positive experience fed by tradition, current interest and future aspirations. Just as an individual person, to be healthy, must have a wholesome acceptance of oneself, so does a nation. Although Canada, which was inhabited by Indians and Eskimos, was first colonized by the French early in the seventeenth century and then by the British, immigrants from various other countries began arriving on Canadian shores as early as 1750. There was even a Canadian of Polish origin in Canada's first Parliament in the House of Commons in 1867.
The history of Canada truly is composed of multi-ethnic and multi-cultural contributions. This is Canada's unique identity. Financial support from all levels of government will be necessary to preserve and develop this identity. Furthermore, I believe that constitutional recognition should be accomplished explicitly in the future by a statement in the Canadian constitution acknowledging the multi-cultural nature of Canadian society and, implicitly, by adopting measures such as a bill of rights which would have the effect of protecting minority rights.

subsubtopic: GRAIN-LEGAL ACTION TO COMPEL GOVERNMENT TO MAKE PAYMENTS UNDER TEMPORARY WHEAT RESERVES ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the other day I intruded myself, perhaps with some trepidation and timidity, into the question of the payments under the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act, and having received the answer that I did from the Minister of

Justice (Mr. Turner) I got my dander up. I thought it was about time members from other parts of Canada interested themselves in a rather delicate subject, because one can turn to the Bill of Rights passed by the British Parliament in 1689 and find therein that he will be-
-assuming and exercising a power of dispensing with and suspending of laws and the execution of laws without consent of Parliament-
That was the name of the game in those days-to see it never happened. Later in that preamble we find:
By levying money for and to the use of the Crown by pretence of prerogative for other time and in other manner than the same was granted by Parliament-
That is the name of the game in Canada, because that is precisely what is happening here. We have been asked in the tax year six months removed to levy moneys for uses of Canada and under the statutes of Canada, and they have been diverted to other purposes: or at least now, since we do run at a deficit, we have been asked to say, "Oh, that was only a mistake. We have to use the money for some other reasons." Sir, that cannot be done.
The fight is joined because the farmers in western Canada have taken the measure of issuing a writ against the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) and serving it on him. And yesterday, in the Toronto Globe and Mail, one finds at page 7 two assistant professors of the faculty of law at Queen's University, Kingston, namely, David J. Mullan and John D. Whyte, writing to say that they have written to the Minister of Justice asking him to give them the right to sue, to see that the law of Canada is obeyed. I talked to those two professors today, and they did not receive an answer from the Minister of Justice. I would have been awfully surprised had I phoned them and found that they had received an answer, and more especially if he had said, "Go ahead, boys; sue the Minister of Finance or the Prime Minister of this country." But that did not happen.
We know the Minister of Justice, for all his posturing, is a lovely fellow, but he still has to posture because in the just society he simply cannot instruct the cabinet on what is the law and what their duties are. Let us take two cases in recent times. One was fought in the British Columbia Supreme Court, before Mr. Justice Norris, on October 19, 1960, where it was held;
It is the duty of members of the executive-
That is the Prime Minister, the Minister of Justice, and so on.
-to obey the law, not to disregard it, and they must ascertain the law in order to obey it.
I am glad to see the Parliamentary Secretary here tonight. He is a nice fellow and I am delighted about his attendance, because I know he has the onerous job of representing a boss who did not have the guts to attend this evening. I quote further:
It is the duty of members of the executive to obey the law, not to disregard it, and they must ascertain the law in order to obey it. Matters of the practice and policy of the government or any department thereof cannot override the duty of obedience to the law, nor will it avail a minister of the Crown to say that he acted on legal advice where it turns out to be wrong.
September 30, 1971

We do not know whether the Minister of Justice gave advice that turned out to be wrong, because we do not have him here tonight. I am sure we will never hear his side of the story until his memoirs are published many years hence.
The fact is there is abuse of the law in this matter. There is a statute which obligates the government of Canada to collect money for a certain purpose. That money was not collected for this purpose. We have the Revised Statutes, and the fact is that the Minister of Justice decided to see that the law we are dealing with tonight was not included in those statutes. In addition to the case I have mentioned in of British Columbia there was a case some years ago in Quebec where Premier Duplessis directed the chairman of the Liquor Licensing Board to see that the bar licence of one Roncarelli of the city of Montreal was not renewed because the individual involved supported Jehovah Witnesses by signing bail bonds. The courts of that day had the guts to stand up, as I hope they always will, and awarded damages and substantial costs against the Premier of the province.
Finally, chapter J-2, section 4(b), provides:
The Minister of Justice shall
(b) see that the administration of public affairs is in accordance with law-
He has not done that in this case. In section 5(d) it is stated that the Attorney General of Canada, which is the same individual, shall-
-have the regulation and conduct of all litigation for or against the Crown for any public department, in respect of any subject within the authority or jurisdiction of Canada-
It shall be written on the tombstone of the present Minister of Justice that because of the schizophrenia of the time he was supposed to do one thing but did another and that this finally caught up with him. I regret, indeed, having to say that in view of the appointment of the hon. gentleman.
